Key File Combines with the run-wide settings include_genera_by_sample TSV with the header columns sample and genus; several rows per sample allowed; a cell may hold A;B adds the genera to include_genera for that sample exclude_genera_file text file, one or more genera per line, separated by ; or , (not by spaces); lines that start with # are skipped, and a # after a genus is read as part of the name adds the genera to exclude_genera for every sample sample_overrides TSV with the header columns sample and mode (required) and include_genera, exclude_genera, discard_no_hit (optional) replaces, for that sample, each setting the row fills in

The run-wide lists come first, the genera of the two genus files are added to them, and then the sample_overrides row is applied. An override's include_genera therefore replaces both the run-wide list and the include_genera_by_sample additions of that sample.

In the example override table below, which is tab-separated, isolate1 keeps every contig and isolate2 loses its Pseudomonas contigs and its contigs without hits. Every other sample follows the run-wide policy.

sample  mode    include_genera  exclude_genera  discard_no_hit
isolate1    off         
isolate2    exclude     Pseudomonas true

An empty cell keeps the run-wide value. Every row needs all its tabs, including those of empty cells, because a missing tab shifts the columns.

When the screen runs, a faulty file stops the run before any job starts. The dry run checks the three files against the samples of the run and stops in these cases.

Checked Stops the run when each file that is set it is not an existing file, or is not UTF-8 text the header line include_genera_by_sample lacks the columns sample and genus, or sample_overrides lacks sample and mode the mode of every sample_overrides row, whatever its sample it is not off, include, exclude or blank (auto gets its own message, with the explanation quoted under Why there is no auto mode) the discard_no_hit cell of a sample of the run it is not true/false, yes/no, on/off, 1/0 or blank the genera of a sample of the run the sample is left in include mode without a genus (the message above)

The messages of the first four checks name the key and the file and, for a bad row, its sample, for example [FunFlux] parameters.decontamination.sample_overrides: sample 'S' has mode 'M' in '<table>'; the mode column must be off, include, exclude or blank (blank keeps the run-wide mode). Without the screen, the files are not read and not checked. A table edited after the dry run is checked again when select_contigs runs, and a faulty one then stops that step, with a Python error in logs/select_contigs_{sample}.log.

A configuration that still has the FunFlux 1.x key parameters.genus and no decontamination block is translated, with a NOTE, as described in Coming from v1. A genus in the v1 key becomes mode: include with that genus, and the NOTE says that include keeps only the contigs BLAST assigned to it. An empty v1 key becomes mode: off, and the NOTE says that FunFlux 1.x then kept the genus with the most contigs, and that v2 makes no automatic choice:

[FunFlux] NOTE: parameters.genus (a v1 key) is empty. FunFlux 1.x kept the genus with the most contigs when parameters.genus was empty; FunFlux v2 has no automatic choice, so every contig is kept (decontamination mode off). To filter, read contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv, then set parameters.decontamination: exclude the contaminant genera, or include the genera that BLAST assigned to the isolate's own contigs.

docs.title: Protected mitochondrial contigs
docs.text:
The contig selector also reads mitochondria/confirmed_mitochondrial.ids, the contigs that screen_mitochondria confirmed from the same BLAST table. It keeps them before any other test, mode: off and discard_no_hit included, with the reason protected_confirmed_mitochondrial.

The protection is needed because BLAST can give a fungal mitochondrion a genus other than the one a genus filter keeps, or no hit at all. The nuclear contigs of a poorly sequenced fungus, for example, can be labelled with a better-sequenced relative, while its mitochondrion, whose reference genome is in core_nt, carries the true genus. Without the protection, include with the relative alone would then remove the mitochondrion.

A protected contig that has no BlobTools row is kept with the genus no-taxonomy. A protected ID that is not in the draft FASTA stops the step (Protected mitochondrial contig(s) were not found in FASTA: ...), which means that the list and the FASTA come from different assemblies.

Only the default mitochondria.mode: separate_confirmed protects the mitochondrion from a genus filter

With mitochondria.mode: report or off, the list of confirmed contigs is empty and nothing is protected. A contig that the contig selector removes cannot come back at the later split.

docs.title: Why there is no auto mode
docs.text:
FunFlux 1.x and BacFlux, the sister workflow for bacteria, have a fourth mode, auto, which keeps one dominant genus and removes every other contig. FunFlux 1.x and BacFlux up to v2.0.1 chose the genus that BlobTools gives to the most contigs. BacFlux v2.1.0 by default chooses the genus that holds the most bases (auto_vote: bp). FunFlux v2 has no auto mode, because BLAST genus labels are unreliable for poorly sequenced fungi.

When core_nt holds few sequences of the isolate's genus, BlobTools gives most of the isolate's contigs the genus of better-sequenced relatives, often several of them, and many short contigs can get no hit at all. In FunFlux 1.x, auto counted contigs, not bases, and the no-hit contigs took part in the vote unless discard_no_hit: true. The winner could therefore be no-hit or a mislabel, and every contig with another label, genuine genome included, was removed.

auto in parameters.decontamination.mode stops every run before any job starts:

[FunFlux] parameters.decontamination.mode: 'auto' is not available in FunFlux. BLAST genus labels are unreliable for poorly sequenced fungi, so auto can remove most of the genome. Use off (the default), read contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv, then exclude the contaminant genera or include the genera that BLAST assigned to the isolate's own contigs.

In the mode column of sample_overrides, auto stops the run with the same explanation, but only when the screen runs, because without the screen that table is not read.

Removal by genus removes genome when the genus calls are wrong

include and exclude remain, because there you name the genera after reading contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv and the composition file. The trap is the true genus. When core_nt holds few of its sequences, BLAST gives it to only a few of the isolate's contigs, and include with the true genus alone removes most of the genome. The warnings in logs/select_contigs_{sample}.log flag such a removal, but with include or exclude the run then goes on to annotate what is left.

The calls also depend on the BLAST hit depth. Keeping more hits per contig changes the bit-score sums, and with them the genus of some contigs (BLAST hit depth).

docs.title: Audit files
docs.text: The contig selector records its decision on every contig in one table, the share of each genus in a composition file, and its warnings in a log.

docs.title: contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv
docs.text:
The decisions table has one row per contig of the BlobTools table, in table order, plus any protected contig without a BlobTools row.

Column Content contig contig name, the first word of the FASTA header assigned_genus the BlobTools genus, no-hit, or no-taxonomy action keep or remove reason one of the codes below

The reason column holds one of these codes.

reason Meaning protected_confirmed_mitochondrial confirmed mitochondrial contig, kept in every mode mode_off mode: off discarded_no_hit no BLAST hit, and discard_no_hit: true included_genus include; genus listed included_genus_alias include; an alias of a listed genus not_included_genus include; genus not listed excluded_genus exclude; genus listed not_excluded_genus exclude; genus not listed

With the default settings, every row reads keep / mode_off, except those of the confirmed mitochondrial contigs, which read keep / protected_confirmed_mitochondrial.

docs.title: Composition file
docs.text:
{sample}_composition.txt has one line per genus, over every contig of the BlobTools table, kept or removed. Each line gives the genus share of the bases and of the contig count, as fractions with two decimals, and the lines are sorted by bases:

<genus>: bases <share of the bases>  contigs <share of the contigs>

The two shares can disagree, because a genus can hold many short contigs while another holds most of the genome.

docs.title: Log messages
docs.text:
The contig selector writes these messages to logs/select_contigs_{sample}.log.

Message Printed when WARNING: N genera each hold at least 5% of this assembly (...). Either the sample is a mixed culture, or one genome is being split across related genera by the BLAST assignment. Check the kept/removed split in contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv before trusting this assembly. two or more genera hold at least 5 % of the bases WARNING: decontamination is discarding X% of the assembly (R of T bp). If the kept assembly then looks incomplete but NOT contaminated, the filter has most likely removed genome rather than contamination. more than 20 % of the bases are removed WARNING: N contigs from BlobTools table were not found in FASTA. the BlobTools table names contigs the FASTA lacks Sample S decontamination mode: M and Kept K of N contig assignments. when the step succeeds, as the last two lines

The warnings change no decision and do not stop the run. They are checked in every mode, so the first one can appear with the default mode: off too.

The step fails in these cases.

The step fails when Message no contig is kept No contigs were kept for sample 'S' with mode 'M'. Check taxonomy assignments and decontamination settings. a protected ID is missing from the FASTA Protected mitochondrial contig(s) were not found in FASTA: ... include has no genus (the dry run normally stops that case first) Mode 'include' requires at least one genus. the BlobTools table has no readable row No contig taxonomy records could be parsed from '<table>'.

Snakemake then deletes the outputs of the step, the decisions table included. Add --keep-incomplete to the command line to keep them for inspection. Snakemake treats files kept this way as finished, so delete them, or add --forcerun select_contigs, before the next run.

docs.title: Changing the policy after a run
docs.text:
Snakemake notices a changed decontamination setting, BLAST hit depth or mitochondrion threshold, and re-runs the steps that use it and every step after them.

Change Re-runs a new decontamination policy select_contigs, the mitochondrion split, QC, ITS and the whole annotation of every sample: hours per sample a new hit depth, nt_version or blast_db path BLAST as well, and every step after it a new mitochondrion threshold the mitochondrion screen and every step after it

A BLAST database or a file-setting table changed in place needs --forcerun

A changed setting re-runs everything after it by itself. A BLAST database updated in place re-runs nothing, so add --forcerun blast_contigs. A table of the three file settings edited in place re-runs nothing either, because Snakemake sees the path, not the content. Add --forcerun select_contigs to apply the edited table.

docs.title: Coverage track
docs.text:
blobtools create requires a BAM file of reads aligned to the draft. Only the read-based modes give a real coverage track.

Mode Reads aligned to the draft Aligner BAM after the run contigs none: the contigs are aligned to themselves minimap2 -a, no preset deleted once BlobTools has read it illumina the trimmed read pairs bowtie2 kept; Qualimap reads it longread, hybrid the filtered long reads minimap2, map-ont or map-hifi per sample kept; Qualimap reads it

In the read-based modes, bowtie2 runs in its default end-to-end mode and minimap2 with the sample's preset. Qualimap's report on the kept BAM is described on Assembly QC.

In contigs mode the coverage values mean nothing

In contigs mode the BAM exists because BlobTools needs one. Each contig is one "read" that maps once, to itself, and BlobTools computes coverage as mapped reads × mean read length / contig length. The value is therefore the mean contig length divided by the contig's own length, below 1 for contigs longer than the mean and above 1 for shorter ones. The contig selector reads only the genus, in every mode.

docs.title: BLAST against core_nt
docs.text:
blast_contigs runs one megablast search per sample, here with the default settings:

BLASTDB=/path/to/blast_db \
blastn -task megablast \
  -query 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_filt.fasta \
  -db /path/to/blast_db/core_nt \
  -outfmt '6 qseqid staxids bitscore pident evalue length qlen slen qcovs qcovhsp sskingdoms scomnames sscinames sblastnames stitle' \
  -num_threads 24 -evalue 1e-5 \
  -max_target_seqs 50 -max_hsps 5 \
  -out 02.assembly/{sample}/contaminants/blastout

BLAST's megablast task looks for highly similar sequences and is much faster than the more sensitive blastn task. directories.blast_db must hold the files below.

File Read by If missing the BLAST database named by parameters.nt_version (default core_nt) blastn BLAST fails taxdb.btd, taxdb.bti blastn, for the organism-name columns those columns read N/A nodes.dmp, names.dmp (NCBI taxdump) BlobTools the dry run stops with MissingInputException in rule blob_json

Without taxdb the run goes on, with N/A for the organism names. The downloads are described on Reference databases.

parameters.nt_version (default core_nt) is the name of the database inside directories.blast_db, either core_nt or nt. Two more settings decide how much BLAST keeps per contig.

Key BLAST option Keeps Default Allowed The dry run prints a NOTE when parameters.blast_max_target_seqs -max_target_seqs database sequences ("subjects") per contig 50 integer ≥ 1 below 5 parameters.blast_max_hsps -max_hsps alignments per subject 5 integer ≥ 1 below 5, unless mitochondria.mode is off

Keep the defaults, 50 subjects with 5 alignments each per contig, because smaller values lose evidence in two ways.

  • BLAST applies -max_target_seqs during the search, not as a final best-N filter, so a small value can lose better matches. BLAST recommends 5 or more.
  • The qcovs column (query coverage per subject), which the mitochondrion screen reads, is computed from the kept alignments only. With -max_hsps 1, BLAST keeps only the single best local alignment per database sequence, so a complete mitochondrial genome that aligns in several blocks can look only half covered.

The evidence behind these defaults, and the effect of the hit depth on the genus calls, are described on BLAST hit depth.

BLAST is the slow step of the screen. On 24 threads it took 40 to 51 minutes for the 42.6 Mb Botrytis cinerea B05.10 assemblies of the validation runs. In contigs mode, every other step of the screen takes seconds.

docs.title: BlobTools: one genus per contig
docs.text:
BlobTools joins the BLAST hits and the coverage track into one table, with a taxon per contig and rank. blob_json runs blobtools create on the draft, the BAM, blastout, nodes.dmp and names.dmp, and blob_table flattens the result:

blobtools view --input blob.blobDB.json --out bestscore --taxrule bestsum --rank all --hits

bestsum adds up the bit scores of all hits per taxon, separately at each rank, and the taxon with the highest sum wins. bestscore.blob.blobDB.table.txt has one row per contig, with these columns.

Columns Content 1 to 5 name, length, GC, N count and coverage (bam0) 6 to 29, four per rank: superkingdom, phylum, order, family, genus and species the winning taxon, its summed score, the number of other taxa with hits and, added by --hits, every competing taxon with its own sum

The contig selector reads only the genus, column 22, and a contig without a BLAST hit has the genus no-hit. The competing taxa show how close a call was.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
The steps on this page write these files to 02.assembly/{sample}/contaminants/. Everything the decision rests on is kept. Only the BlobTools intermediates and, in contigs mode, the BAM are deleted.

File Kept Content blastout yes megablast hits, one line per alignment, the 15 columns of -outfmt above bestscore.blob.blobDB.table.txt yes BlobTools table, one row per contig contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv yes genus, action and reason per contig {sample}_composition.txt yes share of bases and contigs per genus contigs.list yes names of the kept contigs contigs_decontam.fasta yes kept contigs with their original headers, 80 bases per line {sample}_map.bam, {sample}_map.bam.bai contigs mode: no; read-based modes: yes coverage track; in the read-based modes Qualimap reads it too blob.blobDB.json, blob.{sample}_map.bam.cov no BlobTools intermediates

The full output tree is on Output files.

docs.title: Functional annotation
docs.text:
Four tools annotate the genes from gene prediction: InterProScan, eggNOG-mapper, antiSMASH and, when it is switched on, SignalP 6. funannotate annotate then merges their results with its own database searches into the final GenBank, GFF3 and table files. This page describes each step, what it needs and what it writes, and lists the final files of the annotation.

---
config:
  themeVariables:
    fontSize: 14px
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 35
    rankSpacing: 35
---
flowchart TD
    PROT([predicted proteins<br/>funannotate/<br/>predict_results/#lt;stem#gt;.proteins.fa]) --> IPR[InterProScan<br/>families, domains<br/>and GO terms]
    PROT --> EGG[eggNOG-mapper<br/>orthologous groups<br/>and descriptions]
    PROT -.->|only with SignalP 6 on| SP[SignalP 6<br/>signal peptides]
    GBK([genome with gene models<br/>funannotate/<br/>predict_results/#lt;stem#gt;.gbk]) --> AS[antiSMASH<br/>secondary-metabolite<br/>gene clusters]
    IPR --> FA[funannotate annotate<br/>adds Pfam, Swiss-Prot,<br/>MEROPS, dbCAN, BUSCO]
    EGG --> FA
    SP -.-> FA
    AS --> FA
    FA --> OUT([funannotate/annotate_results/<br/>final GenBank, GFF3 and<br/>#lt;stem#gt;.annotations.txt])

Paths below are relative to 04.annotation/{sample}/, except those starting with 00.resources/, 04.annotation/ or logs/, which are relative to the output folder. <stem> is <Genus_species>_{sample}, the file stem of gene prediction.

The table lists the rules that run for each sample, with the files each one reads and writes:

Rule, as the console and the log files name it Tool Reads Writes Threads (at most) iprscan_annotation InterProScan 5, installed by the user (tested with 5.78-109.0), with OpenJDK 11.0.30 and Python 3.11.15 funannotate/predict_results/<stem>.proteins.fa iprscan/interproscan_out.xml 10 eggnog_annotation eggNOG-mapper 2.1.13 with DIAMOND 2.0.15 the same proteins eggnog/ 12 antismash_annotation antiSMASH 8.0.4 funannotate/predict_results/<stem>.gbk antismash/ 12 signalp6_annotation, optional SignalP 6 from the user's archive the same proteins signalp6/prediction_results.txt parameters.signalp6.torch_num_threads (8), at most resources.threads funannotate_annotation funannotate annotate 1.8.17 all of the above funannotate/annotate_results/, .annotation_complete.txt 12 cleanup rm .annotation_complete.txt .cleanup_complete.txt 1

InterProScan is the longest step, usually a few hours for a fungal proteome, while the other tools take minutes to about an hour each. The eggNOG-mapper rule is capped at 12 threads so that, with --cores 22 or more, it runs beside InterProScan instead of waiting for it. The run time of a whole sample is given on Run time.

Terms used on this page

<stem> the shared start of funannotate's file names, <Genus_species>_{sample}, such as Fusarium_graminearum_SAMPLE1; the species comes from the annotation parameter table lookup service the EBI online service that returns InterProScan matches already computed for known proteins; it receives checksums, not sequences, and saves run time NOTE a line starting [FunFlux] NOTE that reports something to check without stopping the run; read them after every dry run scaffold_N the name funannotate sort gives each contig, scaffold_1 being the longest; nothing is joined, and the gene models refer to these names secretome the predicted secreted proteins, which funannotate annotate lists from the SignalP 6 result in annotations.secretome.txt and the Secreted column; none without SignalP 6 model weights the trained numbers that make up a model, such as the SignalP 6 model funannotate database the frozen snapshot of funannotate's data, such as Swiss-Prot, Pfam, the BUSCO set and stored AUGUSTUS models, downloaded once from Zenodo into directories.funannotate_db

docs.title: InterProScan
docs.text:
InterProScan looks for known protein families and domains in every predicted protein. Rule iprscan_annotation runs it as follows:

/path/to/interproscan-5.78-109.0/interproscan.sh -i <stem>.proteins.fa -f XML -goterms -pa \
  -cpu {threads} -T iprscan/tmp -o iprscan/interproscan_out.xml

-goterms adds the Gene Ontology terms of the matches, and -pa the pathway annotation.

InterProScan is not on bioconda and takes about 50 GB once set up, so you install it yourself and name its interproscan.sh in files.iprscan. The rule runs it in a conda environment that provides Java 11 and the Python 3 that InterProScan runs for seven of its analyses, listed in the table below. The installation is described on Licensed and external tools.

Before and after InterProScan, the rule checks its input and its output, so that an empty or cut-off XML never reaches funannotate annotate:

  • Before InterProScan, the rule takes the first *.proteins.fa in funannotate/predict_results/, and stops with Could not find a *.proteins.fa file in ... when there is none. It then deletes an old XML.
  • After InterProScan, it checks that the XML parses and that its root element is protein-matches. Otherwise it stops with InterProScan XML validation failed for <path>: ....

When InterProScan fails, the rule starts the job once more before the run stops, and logs/iprscan_annotation_{sample}.log keeps the last attempt only.

InterProScan's working folder, iprscan/tmp/ (-T in the command), stays after the run, empty or nearly so.

The command selects no analyses (no -appl), so every analysis of the installation runs. With 5.78-109.0, that is every analysis of the download except the three with licensed components:

Analyses Which run AntiFam, CDD, Coils, FunFam, Gene3D, HAMAP, MobiDBLite, NCBIfam, PANTHER, Pfam, PIRSF, PIRSR, PRINTS, PROSITE patterns, PROSITE profiles, SFLD, SMART and SUPERFAMILY of these, run with the Python 3 of the conda environment FunFam, Gene3D, HAMAP, MobiDBLite, PANTHER, PIRSR and PROSITE profiles switched off in the InterProScan download, because they contain licensed components Phobius, SignalP and TMHMM

Signal peptides come instead from SignalP 6, when it is switched on.

InterProScan first asks EBI's precalculated match lookup service for the matches EBI has already computed for known proteins, sending it checksums of the protein sequences, not the sequences. The service answers only the newest release, 5.78-109.0, the last InterProScan 5, and refuses older ones (you cannot use this match lookup service).

The lookup is a shortcut, not a requirement. When the service answers, InterProScan computes only the proteins the service does not know. When the computer has no internet, or the service refuses the installation, InterProScan prints Pre-calculated match lookup service failed - analysis proceeding to run locally and computes every match itself.

With or without the service, the matches are the same, but without it the run takes longer. The service returns EBI's e-values, which for the same match can differ from locally computed ones, and very small ones come back as 0.0. FunFlux leaves the service on, by not passing InterProScan's -dp.

The lookup service saves less time for a new isolate

On B. cinerea B05.10, with 11,728 distinct proteins and 10 threads, InterProScan took about 1 hour with the service and 5 hours without. In a check made in October 2026, 500 distinct proteins were drawn at random from the annotation of B05.10, and 500 from that of Cordyceps cateniannulata GXU-8616. The annotation of GXU-8616 has 10,924 predicted proteins, 10,888 of them distinct. The service already knew 471 of the 500 from B05.10 (94 %), but only 5 of the 500 from GXU-8616 (1 %). B05.10's proteins are public, so the service knew most of them, and for a new isolate the gain is smaller.

docs.title: eggNOG-mapper
docs.text:
eggNOG-mapper annotates the predicted proteins it can place in eggNOG orthologous groups, from what is known about those groups. Rule eggnog_annotation runs it with DIAMOND:

emapper.py -i <stem>.proteins.fa --output_dir eggnog --cpu {threads} -m diamond \
  --data_dir /path/to/eggnog_db --output {sample} --temp_dir eggnog/eggnog_tmp --override

DIAMOND searches eggnog_proteins.dmnd, and the annotation comes from eggnog.db. Both lie in directories.eggnog_db, which holds the eggNOG 5.0.2 data of eggNOG-mapper 2.1.13 (48 GB). Its download is described on Reference databases.

A missing eggNOG folder only gives a NOTE, and the run fails later

When the folder named by directories.eggnog_db does not exist, FunFlux only prints a NOTE before any job starts. eggnog_annotation reads the predicted proteins, so it fails only after gene prediction has run.

eggNOG-mapper writes its results to eggnog/:

File in eggnog/ Content {sample}.emapper.annotations one row per annotated protein: seed ortholog, eggNOG orthologous groups, COG category, description, preferred gene name, GO terms, EC number, KEGG orthology, pathways and modules, CAZy family and Pfam domains. funannotate annotate reads this file {sample}.emapper.hits, {sample}.emapper.seed_orthologs the search results behind it eggnog_tmp/ the scratch folder; Snakemake deletes it when the job ends

docs.title: antiSMASH
docs.text:
antiSMASH looks for secondary-metabolite gene clusters, groups of neighbouring genes that together make a secondary metabolite. Rule antismash_annotation runs it on the GenBank file of the genome with its predicted genes:

antismash --taxon fungi --output-dir antismash --output-basename antismash \
  --databases 00.resources/antismash/databases --genefinding-tool none --cpus {threads} \
  funannotate/predict_results/<stem>.gbk

--taxon fungi selects the cluster detection rules antiSMASH has for fungi. --genefinding-tool none makes antiSMASH use the genes of the GenBank file instead of predicting its own, so the clusters lie on the same gene set as the rest of the annotation. antismash/ holds the interactive report index.html, the antismash.gbk that funannotate annotate reads, antismash.json, antismash.zip and one GenBank file per region, named scaffold_N.regionNNN.gbk.

The database is 00.resources/antismash/databases/, made once per output folder by one of two rules, as directories.antismash_db decides:

directories.antismash_db Rule What happens empty (default) antismash_db download-antismash-databases --database-dir 00.resources/antismash/databases. The database folder of antiSMASH 8.0.4 is 9.4 GB. Kept for later runs on the same output folder; a new output folder downloads it again a folder that holds clusterblast/ antismash_db_local 00.resources/antismash/databases/ is filled with one symbolic link per entry of that folder. Nothing is downloaded or copied, and the folder is only read

Naming a folder therefore lets several output folders share one copy, instead of downloading 9.4 GB for each.

A named folder that does not exist or holds no clusterblast/ stops the run before any job starts. FunFlux checks nothing more: antiSMASH checks the programs and database files of its modules when it starts, and stops if one is missing.

docs.title: SignalP 6 (optional)
docs.text:
SignalP 6 predicts signal peptides, which send a protein into the secretory pathway, the route that secreted proteins take out of the cell. funannotate annotate turns the result into the secretome, the list of secreted proteins. SignalP 6 is off by default. To switch it on, set a mode and name the archive:

Key Default Effect parameters.signalp6.mode off fast, slow or slow-sequential switches SignalP 6 on and chooses the model files.signalp6_archive empty absolute path to the SignalP 6 archive downloaded from DTU; required when the mode is not off parameters.signalp6.archive_sha256 empty SHA-256 of the archive (sha256sum <archive>), compared before the installation parameters.signalp6.torch_num_threads 8 threads of the rule, passed to PyTorch; a value above resources.threads is lowered to it, with a NOTE parameters.signalp6.batch_size 10 proteins per batch (--bsize); raise it only after checking the memory

The archive must contain the model of the mode, so a fast archive such as signalp-6.0i.fast.tar.gz works only with mode: fast.

Rule install_signalp6 runs once per output folder. In this order, it:

  1. checks the SHA-256 of the archive
  2. unpacks the archive, refusing paths that would leave the scratch folder
  3. checks that the model of the mode is there
  4. installs the SignalP package into the signalp6 environment (Python 3.10.13, PyTorch 1.13.1, CPU only) without downloading anything
  5. moves the package with its model weights to 00.resources/signalp6/package/ (1.6 GB with the fast model)
  6. writes 00.resources/signalp6/installation.json

Its log is logs/install_signalp6.log. Licensed and external tools explains how to obtain the archive, and describes the installation in detail.

Rule signalp6_annotation then runs for each sample:

signalp6 --fastafile <proteins, headers cut to the ID> --organism eukarya \
  --output_dir <scratch folder> --format none --mode <mode> --torch_num_threads {threads} \
  --bsize <batch_size> --model_dir 00.resources/signalp6/package/<model folder>

Around the command, the rule does the following:

  • Before SignalP 6, it checks that SignalP 6 is still installed in its conda environment. A rebuilt environment (a changed environment file, another --conda-prefix, a deleted .snakemake/conda) has lost it. The rule then stops and asks you to delete 00.resources/signalp6/installation.json, so that install_signalp6 installs SignalP 6 again.
  • Also before SignalP 6, it cuts the protein headers to the transcript ID, the ID by which funannotate matches the results. An empty or repeated ID stops the rule.
  • After SignalP 6, it checks the result (not empty, a # SignalP-6 line, at least five tab-separated columns), and only then replaces signalp6/ with the new results.

The folder signalp6/ then holds:

File in signalp6/ Content prediction_results.txt one row per protein: ID, prediction (SP for a signal peptide, OTHER for none), the probabilities and the cleavage site output.gff3, region_output.gff3, output.json, processed_entries.fasta SignalP 6's other result files proteins.for_signalp.faa the copy of the proteins with headers cut to the transcript ID

funannotate annotate writes the proteins with a signal peptide to funannotate/annotate_misc/annotations.secretome.txt and to the Secreted column. When that file is missing, funannotate_annotation stops with Funannotate did not create annotations.secretome.txt from the supplied SignalP 6 results.

SignalP 6 in the output folder may not be redistributed

00.resources/signalp6/package/ contains SignalP 6 with its model weights, which may not be redistributed. Remove it before sharing an output folder. The licences are listed on Licensing.

docs.title: funannotate annotate
docs.text:
funannotate annotate builds the final annotation from the results of the four tools. Rule funannotate_annotation runs it as follows:

funannotate annotate -i funannotate --antismash antismash/antismash.gbk \
  --iprscan iprscan/interproscan_out.xml --eggnog eggnog/{sample}.emapper.annotations \
  [--signalp signalp6/prediction_results.txt] --cpus {threads}

To these results it adds its own searches against the funannotate database:

Database What it finds Searched with Pfam 38.2 protein domains HMMER UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot 2026_03 curated proteins, for gene and product names DIAMOND MEROPS 12.5 peptidases DIAMOND dbCAN, HMMdb V11 carbohydrate-active enzymes HMMER

It also searches the BUSCO dikarya models. These are always dikarya, because parameters.prediction.busco_db is passed to funannotate predict only. funannotate annotate combines gene and product names from UniProt and eggNOG-mapper with its Gene2Product list 1.99, and compares the antiSMASH clusters with MIBiG 1.4.

Four further points concern this step:

  • PATH is cut down to the funannotate environment plus /usr/bin:/bin, so an eggNOG-mapper or SignalP installed elsewhere on the computer cannot add results the configuration did not ask for.
  • funannotate annotate skips Phobius (Skipping phobius predictions), so the Membrane column of <stem>.annotations.txt stays empty.
  • No NCBI submission template (--sbt) is passed, so the .sqn file carries funannotate's default.
  • funannotate annotate keeps a copy of the InterProScan XML as funannotate/annotate_misc/iprscan.xml.

docs.title: The final files
docs.text:
The final annotation is in funannotate/annotate_results/. It holds the annotated genome as GenBank and GFF3 files and as one table row per transcript, the sequences, the counts, and the files a GenBank submission needs. Most files are named <stem>.*, for example Fusarium_graminearum_SAMPLE1.*:

File Content <stem>.gbk the annotated genome in GenBank format <stem>.gff3 gene models with product names and notes (eggNOG, SignalP and other evidence) <stem>.proteins.fa proteins, one per mRNA <stem>.cds-transcripts.fa, <stem>.mrna-transcripts.fa coding sequences, transcripts <stem>.annotations.txt one row per transcript: gene and transcript ID, position, name, product, EC number, BUSCO, Pfam, InterPro, eggNOG, COG, GO terms, Secreted, Membrane, protease (MEROPS), CAZyme, antiSMASH, notes, and the sequences <stem>.clusters.txt the genes of each antiSMASH cluster with their annotation and MIBiG hits <stem>.stats.json counts: assembly statistics, genes, mRNAs, tRNAs, and the proteins with each kind of functional annotation <stem>.scaffolds.fa the annotated genome (scaffold_N) <stem>.tbl, .sqn, .agp, .contigs.fsa, .discrepency.report.txt files for a GenBank submission: the feature table, the submission file and the discrepancy report of tbl2asn 25.7, and an AGP file with the contigs split at gaps Gene2Products.must-fix.txt, Gene2Products.need-curating.txt, Gene2Products.new-names-passed.txt funannotate's checks of the product names for a GenBank submission

The counts in <stem>.stats.json vary slightly from run to run, because the gene models do (see Gene prediction).

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Rule cleanup runs last for each sample and removes three kinds of leftovers from the top of 04.annotation/{sample}/: the clean_* scratch folders of an interrupted funannotate clean, *.log files and genome.fixedproducts. It lists what it removed in logs/cleanup_{sample}.log and writes the marker .cleanup_complete.txt.

Everything else stays, so the 04.annotation/ folder of a finished sample holds several GB, most of it funannotate's working files and two copies of the InterProScan XML. See Disk use.

docs.title: Gene prediction
docs.text:
FunFlux predicts the protein-coding and tRNA genes of each sample with funannotate predict 1.8.17, on the soft-masked genome from repeat masking. Tiberius, a gene finder that is not trained on your genome, runs first and adds its gene models to the evidence. Two checks run before the prediction, so that a wrong AUGUSTUS model or an expired GeneMark-ES key stops the run early instead of hours into it. Read this page to choose the AUGUSTUS model of each sample, to decide whether GeneMark-ES and Tiberius run, and to interpret the gene models and their files.

---
config:
  themeVariables:
    fontSize: 14px
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 35
    rankSpacing: 35
---
flowchart TD
    MASK([contigs_mask.fasta<br/>repeats in lowercase]) -.->|"only with GeneMark-ES on"| GM[GeneMark-ES licence check<br/>genemark_check]
    MASK --> TIB[Tiberius<br/>on by default]
    TIB --> TGFF([tiberius.evm.gff3])
    TAB([annotation table<br/>species, proteins,<br/>AUGUSTUS model]) --> AUG[AUGUSTUS model check<br/>augustus_model_check<br/>named model in the database?]
    GM -.-> FP[funannotate predict]
    TGFF --> FP
    MASK --> FP
    AUG --> FP
    TAB --> FP
    FP --> OUT([funannotate/predict_results/<br/>gene models, proteins,<br/>GenBank file])
    OUT --> FA[functional annotation]

One rule, funannotate_prediction, makes the gene models with funannotate predict. The other rules prepare its evidence or check its settings:

Rule, as the console and the log files name it What it does augustus_model_check checks the AUGUSTUS model of column 4 of the annotation parameter table, files.annotation_params (The AUGUSTUS model) genemark_check runs GeneMark-ES on a slice of the genome to catch an expired licence key (GeneMark-ES and the licence check) tiberius_model, tiberius_prediction, tiberius_gff3 download the Tiberius model, predict genes, convert them for funannotate (Tiberius) funannotate_prediction runs funannotate predict on 04.annotation/{sample}/contigs_mask.fasta, one sample at a time, with all resources.threads

The output folder of funannotate predict, 04.annotation/{sample}/funannotate/, feeds every step of the functional annotation.

Terms used on this page

soft-masking writing repeats in lower case, so that gene finders can treat them differently without losing the sequence annotation parameter table the tab-separated file named by files.annotation_params, one row per sample: name, species, a protein FASTA of related fungi and, optionally, an AUGUSTUS model funannotate database the frozen snapshot of funannotate's data, such as Swiss-Prot, Pfam, the BUSCO set and stored AUGUSTUS models, downloaded once from Zenodo into directories.funannotate_db stored AUGUSTUS model the AUGUSTUS parameters trained earlier for one species, kept in trained_species/ of the funannotate database; named in column 4, they are used as they are BUSCO set the BUSCO genes funannotate looks for to train SNAP, GlimmerHMM and, without a stored AUGUSTUS model, AUGUSTUS: dikarya (dikarya_odb9) unless parameters.prediction.busco_db names another EVidenceModeler the program inside funannotate predict that builds one consensus gene per locus from the gene finders and protein alignments, weighting each source's votes ab initio said of a gene finder that predicts genes from the DNA sequence with a trained model, such as AUGUSTUS or SNAP; EVidenceModeler counts Tiberius apart licence key the file ~/.gm_key that GeneMark-ES needs; it expires one year after download, and an expired key stops the run at genemark_check, before gene prediction

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
funannotate predict builds the gene models from the evidence below. The annotation table chooses the proteins and the AUGUSTUS model of each sample, and the configuration chooses the rest for every sample.

Evidence Where it comes from Set by the genome, repeats in lowercase, contigs named scaffold_N repeat masking parameters.masking_method proteins of related fungi column 3 of the annotation table files.annotation_params UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot 2026_03 (uniprot_sprot.fasta, 575,748 proteins) the funannotate database directories.funannotate_db a stored AUGUSTUS model, if any (see The AUGUSTUS model) column 4 of the annotation table: one of the models the funannotate database holds; empty or - trains AUGUSTUS on this genome files.annotation_params, parameters.prediction.augustus_optimize a BUSCO set, to find conserved genes on which SNAP and GlimmerHMM (and AUGUSTUS, when column 4 is empty) are trained the funannotate database: dikarya (BUSCO dikarya_odb9, 1,312 genes) is the only set it comes with parameters.prediction.busco_db GeneMark-ES, optional and licensed the user's installation directories.genemark_dir, parameters.genemark.mode Tiberius's gene models, on by default Tiberius parameters.tiberius.mode

dikarya, the only BUSCO set the funannotate database comes with, suits fungi of the Dikarya. For a fungus outside the Dikarya, add another BUSCO set, such as fungi, to the funannotate database first and set prediction.busco_db to its name. When the database is on disk and the named set is not in it, the run stops before any job starts, with [FunFlux] parameters.prediction.busco_db: '<name>' is not in the funannotate database at '<db>'. Add it with FunFlux's funannotate conda environment activated ('Other BUSCO sets for gene prediction' in the documentation shows how to find it): funannotate setup -i busco -b <name> -d <db> -w. Other BUSCO sets for gene prediction shows how to find and activate that environment.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
Rule funannotate_prediction runs this command for each sample, shown here with a stored AUGUSTUS model in column 4 and Tiberius on:

funannotate predict -i contigs_mask.fasta -o 04.annotation/{sample}/funannotate \
  -s "<species>" --name {sample} --strain {sample} \
  --augustus_species <augustus_species> \
  --other_gff 04.annotation/{sample}/tiberius/tiberius.evm.gff3:1 --busco_db dikarya \
  --protein_evidence <proteins> /path/to/funannotate_db/uniprot_sprot.fasta \
  --cpus {threads}

The annotation table and the Tiberius setting change the command. Column 4 decides whether a stored AUGUSTUS model is used or AUGUSTUS is trained on the genome, and tiberius.mode decides whether Tiberius's gene models are part of the evidence:

Setting Effect on the command column 4 of the annotation table names a stored AUGUSTUS model --augustus_species <augustus_species>, as above column 4 empty --augustus_species is left out; --optimize_augustus takes its place when parameters.prediction.augustus_optimize is true parameters.tiberius.mode: on (the default) --other_gff <file>:1 hands funannotate Tiberius's gene models with weight 1 parameters.tiberius.mode: off --other_gff is left out

Before the command, the rule sets FUNANNOTATE_DB, cuts PATH down to the funannotate environment plus /usr/bin:/bin, and clears GENEMARK_PATH unless GeneMark-ES is enabled. A GeneMark-ES installed elsewhere on the computer is therefore never used by accident.

docs.title: What funannotate predict does
docs.text:
funannotate predict turns the evidence into gene models in the following steps:

Step Tools align the protein evidence to the genome DIAMOND 2.2.4, then Exonerate 2.4.0 self-train on the genome and predict (when enabled) GeneMark-ES find conserved genes for training BUSCO, with prediction.busco_db predict with the stored AUGUSTUS model of column 4, or, with column 4 empty, train on the BUSCO models first AUGUSTUS 3.5.0 train on the BUSCO models and predict SNAP 2017_03_01, GlimmerHMM 3.0.4 combine into one consensus EVidenceModeler 1.1.1 drop models shorter than 50 amino acids or spanning a gap; the repeat filter drops models that lie for at least 90 % in a masked (lowercase) repeat or whose protein matches a transposable element funannotate find tRNA genes tRNAscan-SE 2.0.13

EVidenceModeler builds one consensus gene per locus from all of this. Every source votes for the exons, introns and gene ends it predicts or supports, each vote multiplied by the weight of the source, and the gene structure with the highest total wins. A weight is a relative trust, so only the ratios between weights matter. funannotate writes the sources, with the kind and the weight it gives each, to predict_misc/weights.evm.txt:

Source in EVidenceModeler Evidence Kind Weight Augustus AUGUSTUS models ab initio (ABINITIO_PREDICTION) 1 HiQ AUGUSTUS models with more than 90 % of their exons supported by the protein alignments; they count here instead of under Augustus other (OTHER_PREDICTION) 2 snap, GlimmerHMM SNAP and GlimmerHMM models ab initio (ABINITIO_PREDICTION) 1 each GeneMark GeneMark-ES models, when GeneMark-ES is on ab initio (ABINITIO_PREDICTION) 1 other_pred1 Tiberius models, when Tiberius is on (fixed in FunFlux) other (OTHER_PREDICTION) 1 exonerate the protein alignments protein (PROTEIN) 1

AUGUSTUS models that the proteins support therefore count double, and every other source counts once. The ab initio sources also score the stretches between genes. HiQ and other_pred1 count only for the exons and introns they predict, not for the stretches between genes.

The log lists where the training of each predictor came from:

augustus     pretrained
genemark     selftraining
glimmerhmm   busco
snap         busco
Word in the log Meaning pretrained column 4 named a stored AUGUSTUS model of the database, which AUGUSTUS uses as it is busco trained on this genome's BUSCO models: SNAP and GlimmerHMM always, AUGUSTUS when column 4 is empty selftraining GeneMark-ES trained itself on the genome

A name that is not in the database would also make funannotate train AUGUSTUS, without a word. FunFlux stops on such a name instead, as The AUGUSTUS model explains.

The GFF3 numbers genes and tRNA genes together, so its gene count is the protein-coding genes plus the tRNA genes.

docs.title: The annotation parameter table
docs.text:
The annotation parameter table and the sample name fill in the parts of the command that differ between samples:

From Option of funannotate predict Effect column 2 -s the species column 3 --protein_evidence the protein evidence, beside Swiss-Prot column 4, if it names a model --augustus_species the stored AUGUSTUS model the sample name --name the locus-tag prefix: genes are numbered SAMPLE1_000001, SAMPLE1_000002, ..., their transcripts SAMPLE1_000001-T1 the sample name --strain adds the sample name to the file stem

The funannotate database comes with 166 stored AUGUSTUS models, and ls /path/to/funannotate_db/trained_species/ lists them. Fungal models among them include aspergillus_fumigatus, aspergillus_nidulans, botrytis_cinerea, fusarium, fusarium_graminearum, magnaporthe_grisea and neurospora_crassa.

NCBI accepts a locus-tag prefix of 3 to 12 letters or digits that starts with a letter, and FunFlux prints a NOTE for a sample name that does not fit. Such a sample runs, but its gene IDs cannot be submitted to GenBank as they are.

docs.title: The AUGUSTUS model
docs.text:
Column 4 of the annotation table decides which parameters AUGUSTUS runs with. The choice matters because AUGUSTUS models with strong evidence (more than 90 % of their exons supported) carry weight 2 in EVidenceModeler. That is the highest weight of any gene finder here, and every other model counts 1.

Column 4 What AUGUSTUS does The log says empty, -, or no fourth column (the default) is trained on this genome's BUSCO models with etraining, AUGUSTUS's training program (a few seconds) augustus busco a stored AUGUSTUS model, such as fusarium_graminearum uses that species' parameters from <funannotate_db>/trained_species/ as they are; it is not trained on this genome augustus pretrained empty, with prediction.augustus_optimize: true the same, then optimize_augustus.pl tunes the model's meta-parameters by 8-fold cross-validation, and AUGUSTUS is trained again (details below) augustus busco

The default, an empty column 4, trains AUGUSTUS on the genome itself and needs no choice. Name a stored AUGUSTUS model instead when you know one that suits the genome, typically one of the same species or genus, or when the genome yields too few BUSCO models for training (below). The choice changes a large share of the final gene models, so FunFlux records it for every sample.

Training AUGUSTUS on fewer than 200 BUSCO models stops the prediction late

Training needs at least 200 BUSCO models (funannotate's --min_training_models, which FunFlux does not change). With fewer, funannotate stops after the protein alignment and the BUSCO search, well into the prediction, with Not enough gene models <N> to train Augustus (200 required), exiting. The dikarya set has 1,312 BUSCO genes, but a fragmented assembly, or a fungus outside the Dikarya with the fungi set (290 genes), can give fewer than 200. Name a stored AUGUSTUS model for such a genome.

With prediction.augustus_optimize: true, optimize_augustus.pl tunes the model's meta-parameters, the settings the quick training keeps fixed, such as the width of the windows around splice sites in which AUGUSTUS learns sequence patterns. It tunes them by 8-fold cross-validation. The test genes, the tenth of the BUSCO models funannotate sets aside for testing, are cut into 8 parts, and each part is predicted by a model trained without it. AUGUSTUS is then trained again. This takes about a quarter of an hour for a 40 Mb genome and uses at most 8 CPUs.

With column 4 empty, funannotate first looks for a stored AUGUSTUS model under the name it gives a newly trained one, <genus>_<species>_<sample> in lower case (beauveria_bassiana_arsef3097). Such a model exists only if someone added an earlier result to the database with funannotate species, as funannotate's last message suggests. If it exists, funannotate uses it as it is instead of training, and FunFlux says so in a NOTE and in the record described below.

Rule augustus_model_check runs right after the funannotate database is ready, long before the gene prediction. It stops the run on a name the database does not hold and gives the closest names it does hold, also in logs/augustus_model_check_{sample}.log. It writes the choice to 04.annotation/{sample}/augustus_model.txt, which the gene prediction copies to the top of its log. When the database is already on disk, the same check runs before any job starts, so a dry run shows the error too. Every dry run prints one line with the choice for each sample, for example:

Column 4 Dry-run line empty AUGUSTUS: ARSEF3097 is trained on its BUSCO genes. a stored AUGUSTUS model AUGUSTUS: ARSEF3097 uses the stored model fusarium_graminearum. either, before the database is downloaded the line ends in (checked once the database is unpacked)

docs.title: GeneMark-ES and the licence check
docs.text:
GeneMark-ES is optional and needs a licence. Two configuration keys decide whether it runs:

directories.genemark_dir parameters.genemark.mode GeneMark-ES names an installation (the folder with gmes_petap.pl) auto, the default; a mode left empty (mode: or mode: "") also means auto, as for the other mode keys used empty any not used any off not used

When it is not used, funannotate runs without it, and the dry run prints GeneMark-ES: off (funannotate runs its no-GeneMark branch). FunFlux v2 was tested with GeneMark-ES, and with mode: off on one public genome (Validation on public genomes). See Licensed and external tools for the installation and the key.

The licence key, ~/.gm_key of the user who runs Snakemake, expires one year after download, and the date of the key file does not tell when. gmes_petap.pl only checks that the file exists, so an expired key would show only when funannotate predict reaches GeneMark-ES, well into the run, with Your license period has ended. With GeneMark-ES on, rule genemark_check therefore runs GeneMark-ES on the first 200,000 bytes of contigs_mask.fasta before the prediction. This check takes about a minute. It stops the run when the licence or the installation fails, and writes its result to 04.annotation/{sample}/genemark_check.txt. The command, its outcomes and its messages are on The licence check before gene prediction.

docs.title: Tiberius
docs.text:
Tiberius (Gabriel et al. 2024) finds genes with a deep neural network joined to a hidden Markov model. A hidden Markov model is the kind of model AUGUSTUS and GeneMark-ES use for the order of exons, introns and the DNA between genes. Unlike them, Tiberius is not trained on your genome. It uses one model, fungi, that its authors trained on many fungal genomes. It needs no licence and no evidence, and it runs whether or not GeneMark-ES does. With both on, both count in EVidenceModeler.

Tiberius is on by default and needs no setting. Three configuration keys control it:

Setting Default Meaning parameters.tiberius.mode on off leaves Tiberius out; the funannotate predict command is then the one without --other_gff links.tiberius_model_link the fungi model on the Tiberius authors' server where the model is downloaded from; required while Tiberius is on parameters.tiberius.model_sha256 the checksum of the model file of 8 February 2026 the SHA-256 the downloaded file must have

Tiberius runs in three rules, from the download of its model to the file funannotate reads:

Rule Runs What it does Writes tiberius_model once per output folder downloads the model archive (about 30 MB), checks its SHA-256 checksum and unpacks it 00.resources/tiberius/model/ tiberius_prediction per sample runs Tiberius 1.1.8 (bioconda; its own conda environment with the CPU build of TensorFlow 2.17) on contigs_mask.fasta, so that the scaffold names are the ones funannotate predict uses 04.annotation/{sample}/tiberius/tiberius.gtf tiberius_gff3 per sample converts that GTF with EVidenceModeler's own converter (augustus_GTF_to_EVM_GFF3.pl) into the file funannotate predict gets with --other_gff 04.annotation/{sample}/tiberius/tiberius.evm.gff3

The fungi model was trained without repeat masking, the kind of model the Tiberius authors recommend as the safer default, so Tiberius runs with --no_softmasking. Tiberius therefore reads lowercase and uppercase letters alike, and contigs_mask.fasta gives it the same input as the unmasked genome. After EVidenceModeler, funannotate's repeat filter removes the gene models that fall in repeats, whatever gene finder they came from (What funannotate predict does). Tiberius also gets --seq_len 100080, the model's own length for the pieces the genome is cut into, which Tiberius 1.1.8 does not take from the model.

The model's address carries no version number, so the authors can replace the file at the same address. A file that does not match the checksum stops the run with a message instead of quietly changing the gene models. To accept a new model, check it, compute its checksum with sha256sum <archive> and put that into parameters.tiberius.model_sha256, as described under Tiberius model.

For a fungal genome of about 40 Mb, Tiberius needs:

Resource Need memory about 16 GB. On a single computer Snakemake does not reserve this memory, so switch Tiberius off on a computer with less free memory. On a cluster the job asks for resources.ram_gb, which must then be at least 16 GB CPU all of resources.threads; roughly half an hour on 24 to 32 threads graphics card not used: Tiberius runs on the CPU

The weight of Tiberius in EVidenceModeler is fixed at 1, the weight of the other gene finders, and other values have not been tested.

The logs are logs/tiberius_model.log, logs/tiberius_prediction_{sample}.log and logs/tiberius_gff3_{sample}.log.

docs.title: Run time
docs.text:
For each sample, the two prediction steps run one after the other:

Step Run time for a fungal genome Tiberius, before funannotate predict about half an hour for a 40 Mb genome funannotate predict usually an hour or more

docs.title: Run-to-run variation
docs.text:
funannotate predict does not give the same gene models twice from the same masked genome and settings. The differences are small, but they change the gene counts and the counts of the functional annotation. Run-to-run differences explains which steps differ, and why.

Compare two runs by coordinates, not by gene IDs

Gene IDs are numbered along the scaffolds, so one model gained or lost renumbers every gene after it. Match the gene models of two runs by scaffold, strand and CDS intervals instead.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
funannotate predict writes its results into 04.annotation/{sample}/funannotate/. In the paths below, <stem> is <Genus_species>_{sample}, for example Fusarium_graminearum_SAMPLE1:

Path in funannotate/ Content predict_results/<stem>.gff3 gene models: genes, mRNAs, exons, CDS, tRNAs predict_results/<stem>.gbk the genome with the gene models, GenBank format; the input of antiSMASH predict_results/<stem>.proteins.fa the predicted proteins; the input of InterProScan, eggNOG-mapper and SignalP 6 predict_results/<stem>.cds-transcripts.fa, .mrna-transcripts.fa coding sequences, transcripts predict_results/<stem>.scaffolds.fa, .tbl, .stats.json the genome, the feature table, counts predict_results/<stem>.discrepency.report.txt, .error.summary.txt, .validation.txt the checks of tbl2asn 25.7 predict_results/<model>.parameters.json the AUGUSTUS parameters used: named after the stored AUGUSTUS model, or <genus>_<species>_<sample> in lower case for a model trained on this genome (beauveria_bassiana_arsef3097.parameters.json) predict_misc/ working files: alignments, the models of each predictor, EVidenceModeler logfiles/ funannotate's own logs, funannotate-predict.log among them

With Tiberius on, 04.annotation/{sample}/tiberius/ holds tiberius.gtf, Tiberius's gene models, and tiberius.evm.gff3, the same models as funannotate hands them to EVidenceModeler.

The functional annotation adds annotate_results/ and annotate_misc/ to the same folder, and annotate_results/ holds the final files.

The rule log is logs/funannotate_prediction_{sample}.log. Like every log, it holds the latest attempt only.

Re-running the prediction deletes the annotation

Snakemake treats funannotate/ as one output and deletes it before funannotate_prediction runs again. funannotate/ holds both the prediction and the final annotation. Whenever the prediction runs again, for example after a change in the annotation table, the annotation is therefore deleted and every annotation step runs again, with slightly different gene models. Copy annotate_results/ elsewhere first if you need to keep it.

docs.title: ITS taxonomy
docs.text:
Stage 03.taxonomy cuts the fungal ITS barcode (ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2) out of the nuclear genome, 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_final.fasta, and classifies ITS1 and ITS2 against UNITE with SINTAX. It runs in every mode, once per sample.

The ITS calls are for you to read, as a check on the identity of each isolate. No later step uses them, and the contig summary only counts the 5.8S genes found.

Terms used on this page

rDNA unit one copy of the repeat SSU-ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-LSU; FunFlux counts one per 5.8S gene found, that is, one per ITS window SSU, 5.8S and LSU the small-subunit, 5.8S and large-subunit rRNA genes of one rDNA unit, which reads SSU-ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-LSU ITS window the stretch cut around one 5.8S gene, 2,000 bp on each side by default (its.window_flank), turned to read from SSU to LSU before ITSx runs profile HMM a hidden Markov model, a statistical model, that describes one sequence family; ITSx searches with such profiles SINTAX the VSEARCH classifier (vsearch --sintax) that names each ITS1 and ITS2 rank by rank against UNITE, with a confidence for each rank confidence (SINTAX) the share of SINTAX's repeated classifications, each on a random subset of k-mers, that give the same name at a rank; not a sequence identity UNITE the reference database of ITS sequences, each with its taxonomy; by default, FunFlux uses the release for all eukaryotes and only its records named to genus

For each sample, three rules run one after the other:

contigs_final.fasta
 └─ its_windows ── one window per 5.8S gene, turned to read from SSU to LSU
     └─ its_extraction ── ITSx cuts ITS1, 5.8S and ITS2 out of each window
         └─ its_classification ── identical copies merged; ITS1 and ITS2 classified
                                   with SINTAX against UNITE (records with a genus)

Two more rules prepare the UNITE reference, once per run. The table lists all five, with the tools they use and the files they read and write.

Rule Tools Reads Writes (in 03.taxonomy/{sample}/ unless a path is given) its_windows nhmmer (HMMER 3.4) with the 5.8S profiles of ITSx 1.1.3, then its_windows.py contigs_final.fasta its_windows.fasta, its_windows.tsv its_extraction ITSx 1.1.3 its_windows.fasta {sample}.ITS1.fasta, {sample}.ITS2.fasta, {sample}.full.fasta, {sample}.summary.txt its_classification its_distinct.py, then VSEARCH 2.30.0 --sintax the three ITSx FASTA files and the UNITE reference {sample}_ITS_copies.txt, {sample}_ITS1_taxonomy.txt, {sample}_ITS2_taxonomy.txt unite_db or unite_db_local, once per run curl and gzip, or a symbolic link links.unite_its_link or directories.unite_db 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.fasta and PROVENANCE.txt unite_identified, once per run unite_identified.py unite_its_sintax.fasta 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.identified.fasta and identified_filter.txt

its_windows.py, unite_identified.py and its_distinct.py use only the Python standard library. Each runs with the pinned Python of its rule's conda environment, Python 3.12.13 in itsx and Python 3.12.15 in vsearch, so these steps need no python command on the machine.

docs.title: Why the genome is cut into windows
docs.text:
ITSx uses profile HMMs to find the end of the SSU, both ends of the 5.8S and the start of the LSU, and cuts ITS1 and ITS2 out between them. The rDNA of a fungus is an array of tandem rDNA units, each SSU-ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-LSU. A long-read assembly can place the whole array on a contig of several megabases, often on the minus strand. Given such a contig whole, ITSx reports the domains in the wrong order ("sequence may be chimeric") and writes nothing.

FunFlux therefore gives ITSx one short window per rDNA unit, turned so that it reads from SSU to LSU. The cause and the design are explained in ITS on long-read contigs.

The windows are cut from contigs_final.fasta in every mode. In contigs mode that is the filtered input FASTA. When the contamination and mitochondrion screen runs, the contigs removed by the decontamination policy are no longer in it. With the default parameters.mitochondria.mode: separate_confirmed, the mitochondrion is not in it either.

docs.title: Step 1: one window per rDNA copy
docs.text:
Rule its_windows finds the 5.8S genes of contigs_final.fasta and cuts a window around each, with two commands:

nhmmer --cpu {threads} --dna -E 0.001 --tblout <hits.tbl> <5.8S profiles> contigs_final.fasta
python its_windows.py --tblout <hits.tbl> --fasta contigs_final.fasta --flank 2000 \
  --out-fasta its_windows.fasta --out-table its_windows.tsv
  1. From ITSx's fungal profile file, ITSx_db/HMMs/F.hmm in the itsx environment, the rule takes every profile with 58S in its NAME line. In ITSx 1.1.3 these are 358 of its 538 profiles, anchored at the start or the end of the 5.8S gene. The count is written to logs/its_windows_{sample}.log. nhmmer then searches contigs_final.fasta with these profiles.
  2. its_windows.py keeps the hits with an E-value of at most 1e-5. The start and end profiles hit each 5.8S gene many times, so the script merges the hits into sites, one site per gene. On each contig and strand, a hit joins the current site when it starts at most 1,000 bp after the end of that site. Around the middle of each site the script cuts parameters.its.window_flank bases on each side (default 2,000), clipped at the contig ends, so a full window is 4,001 bp. A window on the minus strand is reverse-complemented.

The merge distance and the E-value limit are fixed, and its.window_flank, a whole number of at least 200, is the only setting. The default 2,000 bp on each side hold the SSU end and the LSU start that ITSx needs, around an ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 region of 0.4 to 1.5 kb.

its_windows.fasta names each window contig:start-end_strand, with 1-based positions on the contig as it is stored in contigs_final.fasta, for example ptg000001l:10001-14001_-. its_windows.tsv has one row per window:

Column Content window_id the FASTA header contig, start, end, strand where the window lies on the contig anchor_hits how many nhmmer hits were merged into the site best_evalue the smallest E-value among them window_length bases; 4,001 unless clipped at a contig end

The table thus has one row per 5.8S gene found, and the contig summary counts these rows per contig as rDNA units. A genome without any 5.8S hit gives an empty FASTA and a table with only the header line, and the rule succeeds. The rule stops if a contig named in the nhmmer table is missing from the FASTA or has another length there.

Two problems with ITSx's profile file stop the rule before the search, each with a message in the log and on the console:

  • a missing or empty F.hmm: [FunFlux] its_windows: ITSx's fungal profile file <env>/bin/ITSx_db/HMMs/F.hmm is missing or empty. Is the job running in its itsx conda environment (--sdm conda), with the pinned ITSx 1.1.3?
  • no profile with 58S in its NAME line: [FunFlux] its_windows: no 5.8S profile found in <env>/bin/ITSx_db/HMMs/F.hmm (no NAME line contains 58S). Does this ITSx version name its 5.8S profiles differently?

docs.title: Step 2: ITSx on the windows
docs.text:
Rule its_extraction runs ITSx on the windows:

ITSx -i its_windows.fasta -o 03.taxonomy/{sample}/{sample} --temp <scratch folder> \
  --preserve T --only_full F --graphical F --complement T --positions F --not_found F \
  -E 0.001 --nhmmer T --cpu {threads}

The options have the following effects:

Option Effect in ITSx 1.1.3 -E 0.001 domain E-value cutoff (ITSx default 1e-5) --nhmmer T search with nhmmer instead of hmmsearch --complement T search both strands (ITSx default); the windows are already oriented --preserve T keep the window names as record names --only_full F report partial regions as well --graphical F, --positions F, --not_found F no graphical output, no table of positions, no list of sequences without ITS

ITSx writes four files:

File Content {sample}.ITS1.fasta one ITS1 record per rDNA unit {sample}.ITS2.fasta one ITS2 record per rDNA unit {sample}.full.fasta ITS1, 5.8S and ITS2 together, one record per rDNA unit {sample}.summary.txt ITSx's own report: windows read, ITS detected on the main or the complementary strand, sequences judged chimeric

The scratch folder given with --temp is deleted when the rule ends. When its_windows.fasta is empty because no 5.8S gene was found, ITSx is not run. The four files are then written empty, and logs/its_extraction_{sample}.log says so.

docs.title: Step 3: copies, distinct sequences and length limits
docs.text:
Rule its_classification first runs its_distinct.py, which reads the three ITSx files and does three things for each region:

  • It groups identical sequences and counts the rDNA units behind each. Upper and lower case, and line wrapping, are ignored.
  • It checks the length against the limits below. A sequence outside them is listed as rejected_too_short or rejected_too_long and not classified.
  • It names the accepted sequences {sample}_ITS1_<n>, {sample}_ITS2_<n> and {sample}_full_<n>, numbered in order of first appearance.
Region Accepted length Classified ITS1 50 to 600 bp (fixed) yes ITS2 50 to 600 bp (fixed) yes full (ITS1, 5.8S and ITS2) at most parameters.its.max_full_length bp (default 1,500, a whole number of at least 400); no lower limit no: it appears in the copies table only

The length limits keep a false ITS2 out of the classification

ITSx can join an SSU end and an LSU start that lie far apart, with only the end of a 5.8S between them, and so report a far too long "ITS2", to which SINTAX would still give a name. ITSx itself calls an ITS region suspiciously long above 1,500 bp, the default upper limit of the full region.

docs.title: Step 4: SINTAX against UNITE
docs.text:
Rule its_classification then classifies the distinct ITS2 sequences against UNITE:

vsearch --sintax <distinct ITS2 sequences> --db 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.identified.fasta \
  --tabbedout 03.taxonomy/{sample}/{sample}_ITS2_taxonomy.txt \
  --sintax_cutoff 0.8 --randseed 1 --threads 1

The same command classifies ITS1. --db is the UNITE reference after the UNITE reference filter described below. With parameters.its.unite_identified_only: false, it is 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.fasta, the whole release. --sintax_cutoff is parameters.its_taxonomy_cutoff (default 0.8), a number above 0 and at most 1.

When no ITS1 or no ITS2 sequence is left, vsearch is not run for that region. The taxonomy file is then created empty, and logs/its_classification_{sample}.log says No ITS1 sequence to classify for sample ... Skipping classification.

SINTAX computes the confidence of each rank by classifying the query many times, each time from a random subset of its k-mers (short words of the sequence), and reports how often the same name came out. Without --randseed, vsearch draws a new random seed in every run, so the same sequence gets slightly different confidences each time. The vsearch manual states that a fixed seed gives the same result only with --threads 1, so FunFlux classifies on one thread.

docs.title: The copies table
docs.text:
{sample}_ITS_copies.txt is tab-separated, with one row per distinct sequence: ITS1 rows first, then ITS2, then full.

Column Content region ITS1, ITS2 or full sequence_id the name of the distinct sequence, for example SAMPLE1_ITS2_1 length bases copies how many rDNA units (windows) carry exactly this sequence status ok, rejected_too_short or rejected_too_long windows the names of those windows, separated by commas

The number of rows per region and their copies show how alike the rDNA units of the assembly are. Two or more rows for one region mean that the units differ, and each distinct sequence is classified on its own. Rows with different classifications can point to a second organism, because windows are cut from every contig of contigs_final.fasta. That file keeps contaminant contigs unless the screen removed them, as described on Decontamination.

copies counts the rDNA units of the assembly, not those of the genome

The copies column counts the rDNA units in the assembly that carry exactly this sequence. A short-read assembly collapses the array into one unit, while a long-read assembly can resolve several.

A rejected_* row has - as sequence_id and is not classified. A line starting with # after the header means that no ITS was found, either because there was no 5.8S hit or because ITSx found nothing in the windows.

docs.title: The taxonomy files
docs.text:
{sample}_ITS1_taxonomy.txt and {sample}_ITS2_taxonomy.txt are tab-separated, without a header, with one line per classified sequence:

Column Content 1 the sequence_id of the copies table 2 the predicted taxonomy from the top rank (d:) down to p: phylum, c: class, o: order, f: family, g: genus, s: species, each rank with its confidence in brackets 3 the strand of the match 4 the ranks of column 2 with a confidence of at least its_taxonomy_cutoff, without the confidences

Column 4 is the call at the cutoff, and column 2 shows how far the lower ranks got. When the phylum is below the cutoff, for example, column 4 stops at d:Fungi, although column 2 may go on to a genus and a species. A different its_taxonomy_cutoff changes column 4 only.

ITS1 and ITS2 are classified separately and can reach different depths, so read both files.

A SINTAX confidence is not a sequence identity

A confidence measures how consistently the k-mer subsets point to one name. A confidence of 1.00 at species level does not mean that the ITS equals a reference sequence.

The species name comes from UNITE and does not reach the annotation. The GenBank files and the funannotate file names carry the species of the annotation parameter table, which can differ from the ITS call.

docs.title: The UNITE reference filter
docs.text:
By default, FunFlux classifies against the UNITE records that name a genus, because the other records can stop the call at d:Fungi. Every UNITE record carries its taxonomy in the header, rank by rank:

>LC784324|SH0155860.10FU;tax=d:Fungi,p:Ascomycota,c:Leotiomycetes,o:Helotiales,f:Sclerotiniaceae,g:Botrytis,s:Botrytis_cinerea;

Many records are identified only down to some rank above the genus, and their taxonomy then stops there: tax=d:Fungi; alone, for example, or a string that ends with the family. In the default release, about a third of the entries have no genus. SINTAX counts how often each name comes out over its repeated classifications (Step 4). A record identified only to the kingdom that is identical to the query is therefore followed as often as the identified records. The result then stops at d:Fungi, even for a genome whose ITS matches well-identified species perfectly. Classified against the records that carry a genus, the same ITS gets its genus and species with the usual confidence values.

The filter is on by default, and the unfiltered result is one setting away:

parameters.its.unite_identified_only SINTAX reference An ITS that matches well-identified species true (default) 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.identified.fasta, the records with a genus gets its genus and species with the usual confidence values false 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.fasta, the whole release; rule unite_identified does not run can stop at d:Fungi

Once per run, rule unite_identified runs unite_identified.py on 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.fasta. It takes a second or two and does three things:

  • It keeps the records whose tax= field holds a genus rank, g: followed by a name. It drops the others, whose taxonomy stops above the genus or whose header has no tax= field.
  • It writes the kept records, unchanged, to 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.identified.fasta, and the two counts, kept_with_genus: <n> and dropped_without_genus: <n>, to 00.resources/unite/identified_filter.txt. logs/unite_identified.log holds a one-line summary and the same counts.
  • It stops the run if no record at all carries a genus, which means the file is not a UNITE SINTAX release.

docs.title: The UNITE reference
docs.text:
FunFlux either downloads the UNITE reference or links a copy you already hold. A local copy in directories.unite_db takes precedence over the download link.

  • Download. While directories.unite_db is empty, rule unite_db fetches the gzip file named by links.unite_its_link. curl -L --fail downloads it and gzip -dc unpacks it on the fly into 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.fasta, so the .gz file is not kept. No checksum is checked. PROVENANCE.txt records the URL, the UTC date, and the md5 and size of the FASTA.
  • Local copy. When directories.unite_db names a folder, rule unite_db_local runs instead. The folder must hold an uncompressed unite_its_sintax.fasta, otherwise the run stops before any job starts. 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.fasta becomes a symbolic link to it, so nothing is copied, and the folder is only read. PROVENANCE.txt records the folder, the UTC date, md5 and size. A NOTE says that links.unite_its_link is not used.

Both rules log to logs/unite_db.log. The files in 00.resources/unite/ are made once per output folder, and later runs on the same output folder reuse them. Whichever rule made the FASTA, unite_identified then filters it as described above.

The table compares the two UNITE releases of version 19.02.2025 (UNITE 10.0).

Release DOI Sequences Size In FunFlux USEARCH/UTAX/SINTAX release for eukaryotes (licence CC BY 4.0) 10.15156/BIO/3301246 266,589, from all eukaryotes, not only fungi 35.7 MB to download, 207 MB unpacked the default link; FunFlux v2 was tested with it Fungi-only release 10.15156/BIO/3301245 168,030

FunFlux v2 was tested with the eukaryote release, but another release in SINTAX format can be given through either key. How to download a local copy is described on Reference databases.

docs.title: Threads and run time
docs.text:
Each of the three steps takes seconds to minutes. Their thread caps are low, so that they can run beside InterProScan, which holds 10 threads for hours:

Rule Threads (at most) its_windows 8 its_extraction 8 its_classification 1

nhmmer and ITSx run with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, so they stay within their thread count. Without these two settings, HMMER's OpenBLAS library starts one thread per CPU core whatever --cpu says, which makes hundreds of threads on a large server.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A fungus whose 5.8S matches none of the 358 profiles gives no window and empty ITS files, and the copies table then holds the # line.
  • The window names use the contig names of contigs_final.fasta. The annotation renames the contigs scaffold_N, as described under funannotate sort, and the annotated_as column of the contig summary links the two names.

docs.title: Mitochondria
docs.text:
A fungal mitochondrial genome, usually some tens of kb and present in many copies per cell, assembles as one more contig. This page describes how FunFlux recognises that contig, sets it apart from the nuclear genome and reports each call. Read it to interpret mitochondria/mitochondrial_screen.tsv or to find out why no mitochondrion was split off.

With the default parameters.mitochondria.mode: separate_confirmed, FunFlux finds the mitochondrial contig with BLAST, protects it from removal by the contig selector and writes it to contigs_mitochondrial.fasta. QUAST, BUSCO, the ITS search and funannotate then read only the nuclear genome, contigs_final.fasta.

The mitochondrion is kept apart because of the genetic code. The mitochondria of most fungi use genetic code 4, in which UGA codes for tryptophan. The mitochondria of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and related yeasts use code 3, which changes AUA and CUN too. The nuclear gene predictor reads UGA as a stop codon and calls false genes on a mitochondrial contig.

Terms used on this page

the screen the contamination and mitochondrion screen of the draft: BLAST against NCBI core_nt, BlobTools, the mitochondrion screen and the contig selector mitochondrion screen rule screen_mitochondria, part of the screen: it confirms mitochondrial contigs from BLAST hits to mitochondrial genomes and, in the long-read modes, the assembler evidence draft assembly (the draft) the assembly the screen examines, before any contig is removed: contigs_filt.fasta in illumina mode and in contigs mode with the screen, assembly.fasta in longread and hybrid contig selector rule select_contigs, the last step of the screen: it keeps or removes each contig by genus, as parameters.decontamination says; the default, off, keeps every contig genus filter the setting parameters.decontamination.mode: include or exclude, under which the contig selector keeps or removes contigs by the genus BlobTools gave them direct hit a BLAST hit to a database sequence whose title says it is a mitochondrial genome; only such hits count as BLAST evidence for the mitochondrion qcovs the BLAST query coverage per subject: the percentage of a contig covered by all kept alignments to one database sequence coverage ratio a contig's depth as the assembler reported it, divided by the median depth of all contigs

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
The mitochondrion screen is one step of the contamination and mitochondrion screen, called the screen on this page. It runs wherever the screen runs, as listed under When the screen runs.

Mode Mitochondrion screen illumina, longread, hybrid always hybrid, Illumina guide assembly its own mitochondrion screen, rule screen_guide_mitochondria, which decides from BLAST alone (Hybrid) contigs with parameters.contigs.screen: true yes contigs without the screen none: nothing is split off, a mitochondrial genome in the input FASTA is annotated as nuclear, and the dry run prints a NOTE saying so
