The mitochondrion screen decides on the draft, before the contig selector runs, so that a genus filter cannot remove the mitochondrion before it is set apart. The split comes last, after polishing. The steps, in order:

Step Rule Reads Writes, in 02.assembly/{sample}/ 1 blast_contigs the draft contigs contaminants/blastout 2 screen_mitochondria blastout, the draft contigs; in longread and hybrid also assembly_evidence.tsv, from assembly_evidence (below) mitochondria/mitochondrial_screen.tsv, mitochondria/confirmed_mitochondrial.ids 3 select_contigs the confirmed IDs, among others contaminants/contigs_decontam.fasta, with the confirmed contigs kept whatever their genus 4 polishing (long-read modes, where it runs), then finalize_assembly the kept contigs contigs_all.fasta 5 separate_mitochondria contigs_all.fasta, the confirmed IDs contigs_final.fasta, contigs_mitochondrial.fasta

In the long-read modes, longread and hybrid, Medaka (ONT samples, unless medaka_model: false) and Polypolish (hybrid) polish the kept contigs before finalize_assembly. PacBio HiFi samples in longread are not polished.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: The mitochondrion screen gives every contig of the draft a class and a reason. BLAST is the evidence in every mode, and the long-read modes add the assembler's evidence.

docs.title: BLAST evidence
docs.text:
The mitochondrion screen reads contaminants/blastout, the BLAST table of the screen described under BLAST against core_nt, and uses only direct organelle hits. In BLAST's terms, each database sequence that a contig matches is a subject. A direct hit is a hit whose subject title says that the subject is a mitochondrial genome. The title must contain one of these phrases, in upper or lower case:

  • mitochondrion, complete genome
  • mitochondrion, complete sequence
  • mitochondrion, partial genome
  • mitochondrion, partial sequence
  • mitochondrial DNA
  • mitochondrial genome

A nuclear gene described as, for example, mitochondrial ribosomal protein L5 mRNA does not count.

For each contig, the mitochondrion screen takes the direct hit with the highest qcovs, the percentage of the contig covered by all kept alignments to that subject. parameters.blast_max_hsps sets how many alignments per subject BLAST keeps. With 1, BLAST keeps only the single best local alignment per database sequence. A complete mitochondrial genome that aligns in several blocks can then look only half covered, and a mitogenome rearranged relative to its closest reference can fall below the threshold. In a run with the screen and with parameters.mitochondria.mode other than off, the dry run prints a NOTE when blast_max_hsps is below 5.

docs.title: Without assembler evidence (contigs, illumina)
docs.text:
In contigs and illumina mode, and on the hybrid guide, BLAST is the only evidence, so a direct hit covering at least 35 % of the contig confirms it.

Best direct hit Class Reason qcovs ≥ min_direct_blast_qcov (35) confirmed_mitochondrial strong_direct_blast qcovs below 35 mitochondrial_candidate weak_direct_blast none not_mitochondrial no_mitochondrial_evidence

very_strong_qcov and min_assembler_coverage_ratio change nothing in these modes, and the coverage that SPAdes writes into its contig names is not used.

docs.title: With assembler evidence (longread, hybrid)
docs.text:
In the long-read modes, rule assembly_evidence, a short step right after the assembly, writes assembly_evidence.tsv beside the assembly. It holds the read depth and the circularity of each contig as the assembler reported them.

Assembler Depth Circularity Also reports hifiasm rd:i tag of the primary contig graph the contig name ends with c (ptg000001c) Flye assembly_info.txt assembly_info.txt repeat status, alternative-haplotype group

The coverage ratio of a contig is its depth divided by the median depth of all contigs. A clean circle is circular, not a repeat and in no alternative group. In these modes a direct hit of at least 35 % needs the support of a high depth or a clean circle, unless it covers 70 % or more. The tests run in this order:

Evidence Class Reason qcovs ≥ 35 and coverage ratio ≥ min_assembler_coverage_ratio (3.0) confirmed_mitochondrial direct_blast_plus_high_coverage qcovs ≥ 35 and a clean circle confirmed_mitochondrial direct_blast_plus_clean_circularity qcovs ≥ very_strong_qcov (70) confirmed_mitochondrial very_strong_direct_blast any other direct hit mitochondrial_candidate direct_blast_without_support no direct hit, circular and coverage ratio ≥ 3.0 mitochondrial_candidate circular_and_high_coverage_without_blast no direct hit, circular circular_unclassified circularity_only no direct hit, coverage ratio ≥ 3.0 high_coverage_unclassified coverage_only none of the above not_mitochondrial no_mitochondrial_evidence

Circularity or depth alone never confirms a contig. Only confirmed_mitochondrial contigs are protected and split off, and the other classes change nothing in the assembly.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The mitochondrion screen has four settings, under parameters.mitochondria. Two act wherever the screen runs, and two only where the assembler reports depth and circularity.

parameters:
  mitochondria:
    mode: separate_confirmed          # off | report | separate_confirmed
    min_direct_blast_qcov: 35
    min_assembler_coverage_ratio: 3.0
    very_strong_qcov: 70
Key Default Allowed Used in mode separate_confirmed off, report, separate_confirmed every mode with the screen min_direct_blast_qcov 35 number > 0 and ≤ 100 every mode with the screen min_assembler_coverage_ratio 3.0 number > 0 longread, hybrid very_strong_qcov 70 number > 0 and ≤ 100 longread, hybrid

With the screen on, the dry run prints the settings in use:

Mitochondrion screen: separate_confirmed (direct BLAST coverage >= 35%, assembler coverage ratio >= 3, near-complete hit >= 70%).

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
parameters.mitochondria.mode decides what FunFlux does with the findings of the mitochondrion screen.

mode Screen table confirmed_mitochondrial.ids Protected from the contig selector contigs_mitochondrial.fasta off every row not_screened, reason screening_disabled empty no empty file report classes and reasons empty no empty file separate_confirmed (default) classes and reasons the confirmed contigs yes the confirmed contigs

Only separate_confirmed protects the mitochondrion and sets it apart

report shows the calls without changing the assembly. With off and report, contigs_final.fasta holds every contig, a mitochondrion included, and it goes through gene prediction. report also leaves the mitochondrion exposed to include, exclude and discard_no_hit.

screen_mitochondria and separate_mitochondria run with every setting of mitochondria.mode, so a finished sample has the same set of files. mitochondria.mode: off does not switch BLAST off, because the rest of the screen still needs it.

The log of screen_mitochondria counts confirmed and selected contigs: Mitochondrial screen: N confirmed call(s); M selected for separation (mode=...).

docs.title: The screen table
docs.text:
mitochondria/mitochondrial_screen.tsv has one row per draft contig, in FASTA order. classification and reason give the call, and the other columns are the evidence behind it.

Column Content contig contig name, the first word of the FASTA header length contig length (bp) classification the class, see the tables above reason the test that decided best_mito_qcovs qcovs of the best direct hit (%); empty without a direct hit direct_mito_hits number of BLAST alignments to mitochondrial-genome subjects best_mito_title subject title of the best direct hit assembler_source hifiasm or flye assembler_circular Y or N assembler_coverage read depth reported by the assembler assembler_coverage_ratio depth divided by the median depth of all contigs assembler_repeat Y or N (Flye) assembler_alt_group alternative-haplotype group (Flye); * for none best_mito_slen length of the best hit's subject, the reference mitochondrial genome (bp) length_ratio length / best_mito_slen, two decimals concatemer_flag Y when length_ratio is above 1.5 and the contig is not recorded as circular, otherwise N; information only

The six assembler_* columns are empty in contigs and illumina mode.

docs.title: The split
docs.text:
separate_mitochondria reads contigs_all.fasta and the confirmed IDs and writes each contig to one of two files. Order and headers are kept, and sequences are written 80 bases per line.

File, in 02.assembly/{sample}/ Content Read by contigs_all.fasta the decontaminated assembly (polished, where polishing runs), mitochondrion included separate_mitochondria contigs_final.fasta the nuclear genome QUAST, BUSCO, ITS extraction, funannotate; the AMR screen when it is on contigs_mitochondrial.fasta the confirmed mitochondrial contigs; an empty file when there are none the AMR screen when it is on, for cytochrome b (Two runs); the contig summary, for the contig names

The contig summary reads the draft and the annotated genome, 04.annotation/{sample}/contigs_sort.fasta, instead of contigs_final.fasta.

The IDs are contig names, the first word of the FASTA header, so every step between the mitochondrion screen and the split must keep them. separate_mitochondria stops before writing anything in two cases:

The rule stops when Message a confirmed ID is missing from contigs_all.fasta ERROR: Confirmed mitochondrial contig(s) are absent from final assembly: ... no nuclear contig would remain ERROR: Mitochondrial split would leave an empty nuclear assembly.

Otherwise the log ends with Mitochondrial split: X mitochondrial and Y nuclear contig(s).

FunFlux does not annotate the mitochondrial genome.

docs.title: Concatemers
docs.text:
An assembler can join two copies of the mitochondrial genome end to end. Such a contig matches the reference over its whole length and is confirmed. The screen table shows it:

length_ratio Reading concatemer_flag about 1 one copy N about 2 two copies joined end to end Y (above 1.5) above 1.5, and the assembler reported the contig as circular a closed circle longer than the reference: a larger genome, or two copies that the assembler joined into one circle (hifiasm did so with the HiFi reads of the validation page: 49,194 bp against 24,712 bp) N

Y marks a likely double copy, but only on a confirmed row. The reason is that the flag is computed for every contig with a direct hit, and a long nuclear contig with a short mitochondrion-like stretch also has a high ratio. In contigs and illumina mode circularity is unknown, and the flag depends on the ratio alone.

FunFlux does not trim a concatemer to one copy

The flag changes nothing: the contig is split off as it is.

docs.title: When no mitochondrion is confirmed
docs.text:
contigs_mitochondrial.fasta is then empty, and a mitochondrion that was assembled stays in contigs_final.fasta and is annotated as nuclear. The screen table shows why:

Finding Meaning What to do a mitochondrial_candidate row with reason weak_direct_blast a direct hit covers less than min_direct_blast_qcov of the contig if the length (usually some tens of kb) and the title fit, set min_direct_blast_qcov to the row's best_mito_qcovs or lower and run again no row with a direct hit core_nt holds no mitochondrial genome close enough nothing to set in contigs and illumina mode; in the long-read modes depth and circularity can only give a candidate or ..._unclassified row blast_max_hsps below 5 qcovs counts only the alignments BLAST kept per subject, with 1 the best one alone set blast_max_hsps: 5

A weak hit or a low blast_max_hsps can be fixed with a setting, but a missing reference genome cannot. A changed threshold re-runs the mitochondrion screen and every step after it, as described under Changing the policy after a run.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
Each sample keeps these files after the run:

File Kept Content 02.assembly/{sample}/mitochondria/mitochondrial_screen.tsv yes one row per draft contig 02.assembly/{sample}/mitochondria/confirmed_mitochondrial.ids yes confirmed contig names, one per line; empty unless separate_confirmed 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_all.fasta yes assembly with the mitochondrion 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_final.fasta yes nuclear genome 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_mitochondrial.fasta yes mitochondrial contigs logs/screen_mitochondria_{sample}.log, logs/separate_mitochondria_{sample}.log yes counts and errors

Without the screen (contigs mode by default), only contigs_final.fasta exists of these. The full output tree is on Output files.

docs.title: Repeat masking
docs.text:
FunFlux prepares the nuclear genome for gene prediction in two steps, the same in every mode. First, funannotate removes short and duplicated contigs and sorts and renames the rest. Then the repeats are soft-masked. The files of both steps are in 04.annotation/{sample}/. Read this page to find out why a contig can be missing from the annotation, how the annotated contigs are named, and which masking method to choose.

contigs_final.fasta
 └─ funannotate clean ── contigs_clean.fasta    short and duplicated contigs removed
     └─ funannotate sort ── contigs_sort.fasta  longest first, renamed scaffold_N
         └─ masking ── contigs_mask.fasta       repeats in lowercase; on to gene prediction

funannotate clean and funannotate sort run in one rule, and the masking in another:

Rule Tools Reads Writes funannotate_preprocess funannotate 1.8.17: clean, then sort 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_final.fasta contigs_clean.fasta, contigs_sort.fasta, contigs_removed_by_clean.txt repeat_masking tantan 51, or RepeatModeler 2.0.8 and RepeatMasker 4.2.3 contigs_sort.fasta contigs_mask.fasta, repeatmasking/

contigs_mask.fasta goes on to gene prediction, where funannotate predict, Tiberius and, when GeneMark-ES is on, its licence check read it. Tiberius gets the same file so that the scaffold names match. Its fungi model was trained without repeat masking, so it reads lowercase and uppercase letters alike, and for Tiberius the genome is in effect unmasked.

Terms used on this page

soft-masking writing repeats in lower case, so that gene finders can treat them differently without losing the sequence scaffold_N the name funannotate sort gives each contig, scaffold_1 being the longest; nothing is joined, and the gene models refer to these names haplotig a contig holding the second copy of a heterozygous region, assembled apart from the first; funannotate clean drops such duplicates when shorter than the N50 scratch a working file or folder that the step which wrote it deletes when that step ends EVidenceModeler the program inside funannotate predict that builds one consensus gene per locus from the gene finders and protein alignments, weighting each source's votes repeat library a FASTA of a genome's repeat families; RepeatModeler builds it from the genome itself, and RepeatMasker then masks the copies it finds random seed the number a program's random choices start from; fixing it makes a later run repeat the same choices

docs.title: funannotate clean
docs.text:
funannotate clean drops contigs before anything is annotated:

funannotate clean -i contigs_final.fasta -o contigs_clean.fasta --cpus <threads>

FunFlux keeps funannotate's defaults. A contig is dropped when:

Condition Option (default) it is shorter than 500 bp -m 500 it contains a character that is not an IUPAC nucleotide code none it contains fewer than four different letters none it is shorter than the assembly N50, and one minimap2 2.31 alignment to a contig of at least N50 length, or to a shorter contig, covers more than 95 % of its length at more than 95 % identity -p 95, -c 95

Only a contig shorter than the N50 can be dropped as a duplicate. Contigs at least as long as the N50 are not tested for duplication, because FunFlux does not use funannotate's --exhaustive option. The duplication test removes, for example, haplotigs that an assembly from a sequencing provider may still contain. Left in, the genes on them would be annotated twice.

The step declares 2 threads, or 1 when resources.threads is 1, and runs that many minimap2 searches at a time (--cpus). Each search starts minimap2's default 3 threads, so the job uses a little more CPU than it declares. The cleaned genome does not depend on the thread count.

When funannotate clean is killed half-way, it leaves a scratch folder, clean_<random>, in 04.annotation/{sample}/. The cleanup step removes it.

logs/funannotate_preprocess_{sample}.log gives the number of input contigs, the number of those longer than 500 bp, and the N50. It also says how many contigs shorter than the N50 were checked for duplication, how many were duplicated, and how many were written to contigs_clean.fasta.

QUAST, BUSCO and the ITS search can count contigs that the annotation leaves out

contigs_removed_by_clean.txt lists, one name per line and in input order, every contig of contigs_final.fasta that is missing from contigs_clean.fasta. An empty file means that nothing was dropped. A dropped contig stays in contigs_final.fasta, so QUAST, BUSCO and the ITS search still count it, but it is not annotated.

docs.title: funannotate sort
docs.text:
Next, funannotate sort gives the contigs the names that the annotation uses:

funannotate sort -i contigs_clean.fasta -o contigs_sort.fasta --minlen 0

sort orders the contigs from longest to shortest and renames them scaffold_1, scaffold_2, and so on. According to funannotate's help, the contigs are renamed because AUGUSTUS can have problems with complicated contig names. --minlen 0 drops nothing, and the sequences are not changed.

contigs_sort.fasta is the genome that the annotation describes, so the assembly results and the annotation name the same contig differently. Which name a contig has depends on the file:

Files Contig names GFF3, GenBank and antiSMASH files scaffold_N: every coordinate refers to a contig of contigs_sort.fasta SignalP 6, InterProScan, eggNOG-mapper none: they report per protein, by transcript ID (SAMPLE1_000001-T1) QUAST, BUSCO and the ITS files the original contig names the contig summary both: its annotated_as column links each contig to its scaffold_N (Contig summary)

Since only names and order change, a contig can also be matched to its scaffold by sequence, or by length where lengths are unique.

docs.title: Masking
docs.text:
Soft-masking writes repeats in lowercase instead of replacing them by N, so no sequence is lost. AUGUSTUS and GeneMark-ES treat the lowercase stretches with caution. SNAP and GlimmerHMM, which funannotate also runs, and Tiberius read lowercase and uppercase letters alike. After EVidenceModeler, funannotate's repeat filter removes the gene models that lie for at least 90 % in a masked repeat or whose protein matches a transposable element, whatever gene finder they came from. See What funannotate predict does.

parameters.masking_method chooses the tools: tantan, which is fast and masks simple repeats only, or RepeatModeler and RepeatMasker, which also mask transposons and other interspersed repeats and take far longer.

masking_method Commands What is masked Run time Threads tantan (default) tantan contigs_sort.fasta > contigs_mask.fasta tandem repeats and low-complexity sequence seconds 1 repeatmodeler_repeatmasker BuildDatabase -name {sample}_rm, RepeatModeler -database {sample}_rm -threads {threads}, then RepeatMasker -pa {threads} -xsmall -lib {sample}_rm-families.fa the repeat families RepeatModeler finds in this genome (interspersed repeats such as transposons), plus simple repeats and low-complexity sequence tens of minutes or more at most 12 (below)

RepeatMasker masks with the library RepeatModeler built from the genome itself, so no Dfam or RepBase library is needed. The library is {sample}_rm-families.fa, or RepeatModeler's consensi.fa.classified when that file is missing or empty. When neither holds a sequence, the rule stops with RepeatModeler did not produce a usable repeat library., so an unmasked genome never passes as a masked one.

The share of the genome that was masked is in the line Genome loaded: ... repeats masked of funannotate predict's log and, with RepeatMasker, in its summary table repeatmasking/contigs_sort.fasta.tbl.

docs.title: RepeatModeler settings
docs.text:
These keys take effect only with masking_method: repeatmodeler_repeatmasker.

Key Default Passed as Effect, from the RepeatModeler 2.0.8 help repeatmodeler_quick true -quick uses the smaller genome samples of RepeatModeler versions before 2.0.4: faster, with the sensitivity of those versions repeatmodeler_ltrstruct false -LTRStruct adds the LTR structural pipeline (LTR_Harvest and LTR_retriever) repeatmodeler_seed empty -srand <seed> fixes the seed of the random choice of genome samples; empty: a seed taken from the clock

Without repeatmodeler_seed, two runs on one genome mask slightly differently

RepeatModeler samples the genome at random, so two runs without a fixed seed build slightly different libraries, and the gene models and everything computed from them differ slightly too. RepeatModeler writes the seed it drew near the top of logs/repeat_masking_{sample}.log, in the line Random Number Seed: <number>. Its help describes -srand as the way to reproduce the sample choice between runs. Whether a fixed seed also gives a byte-identical masked genome has not been tested.

repeat_masking declares at most 12 threads and passes them to RepeatModeler as -threads and to RepeatMasker as -pa. RepeatMasker's -pa counts parallel batches, and each batch can run several RMBlast threads, so RepeatMasker may use more CPUs than 12.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
contigs_mask.fasta goes on to gene prediction, and the other files record what was dropped, renamed and masked.

File, in 04.annotation/{sample}/ Content Read by contigs_clean.fasta the genome after funannotate clean, original contig names you contigs_removed_by_clean.txt the contigs clean dropped; empty if none you contigs_sort.fasta sorted and renamed scaffold_N: the genome that is annotated repeat_masking, contig_summary contigs_mask.fasta contigs_sort.fasta with repeats in lowercase funannotate_prediction, genemark_check, tiberius_prediction repeatmasking/ deleted and created anew at every start of the rule; empty with tantan. With RepeatModeler: the BLAST database {sample}_rm.*, the library {sample}_rm-families.fa with its alignments .stk, RepeatModeler's working folder RM_*, and RepeatMasker's contigs_sort.fasta.out (every masked repeat), .tbl (masked bases by repeat class) and .masked you

The logs of the two steps are logs/funannotate_preprocess_{sample}.log and logs/repeat_masking_{sample}.log.

docs.title: Report
docs.text:
The MultiQC report, 06.report/multiqc_report.html, gathers the QC results of all samples of a run into one page. MultiQC 1.33 makes it in rule multiqc, once per run, when the QC results, the contig summary and, with the AMR screen on, the AMR table of every sample are ready. The contig summary waits for the finished annotation, so the report is one of the last jobs of a run. This page describes what MultiQC reads, how the rows are named, which numbers the report shows and which files rule multiqc writes. Read it to find a sample's row in the report or the file behind a number.

Terms used on this page

General Statistics table the MultiQC summary table; for an assembly it shows the N50, the length and BUSCO's complete single-copy and missing counts draft assembly (the draft) the assembly before the contamination and mitochondrion screen removes any contig, such as contigs_filt.fasta or assembly.fasta; the contig summary describes it guide assembly the SPAdes assembly of the Illumina reads; it is screened, and only the pairs that map to it go on contig summary the table 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/contig_summary.tsv: one row per contig of the draft, with its evidence (telomeres, depth, rDNA units, genes) and a verdict verdict (contig summary) the label the contig summary gives each draft contig, one of ten such as chromosome, chromosome_arm, rDNA_array or mitochondrion, with its reasons AMR screen the optional step, off by default (parameters.amr.chroquetas), in which ChroQueTas looks in each genome for the changes FungAMR lists for the species; results in 05.amr/ target protein a protein whose FungAMR positions ChroQueTas checks, such as Beta-tubulin or Cyp51 verdict (AMR screen) the reading of FungAMR's evidence for a change or a target: resistance, conflicting, no resistance, unknown, wild type, or not compared for a position

docs.title: What feeds it
docs.text:
QUAST, BUSCO and the contig summary feed the report in every mode. The read and mapping QC depend on the mode, and the AMR table appears only with the AMR screen on:

Tool What MultiQC reads Modes fastp 1.0.1 01.reads/{sample}/illumina/{sample}_fastp.json illumina, hybrid NanoPlot 1.46.2 01.reads/{sample}/long/raw_qc/, filtered_qc/ ({sample}_NanoStats.txt) longread, hybrid Qualimap 2.3 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/qualimap/; in hybrid also guide/eval/qualimap/ illumina, longread, hybrid QUAST 5.3.0 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/quast/; in hybrid the report holds the guide assembly and the final genome, two rows all BUSCO 6.0.0 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/busco/ all FunFlux contig summary 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/contig_summary_mqc.tsv: one row per contig of the draft assembly, with its verdict all FunFlux AMR screen (ChroQueTas) 05.amr/{sample}/amr_summary_mqc.tsv: one row per target protein of the species, with the FungAMR mutations found and a verdict on resistance all, with parameters.amr.chroquetas: on

The ITS taxonomy and the annotation are not in the report. Their results are in 03.taxonomy/ and 04.annotation/.

QUAST, BUSCO and Qualimap themselves are described under Assembly QC. The pages of the individual modes, reached from Modes, describe fastp and NanoPlot. The contig summary is described under Contig summary, and the AMR table under Antifungal resistance mutations.

A failed QUAST, Qualimap or NanoPlot run does not stop the workflow

The row of the sample concerned is then missing from the report. A failed MultiQC run, on the other hand, stops the workflow.

docs.title: Sample names
docs.text:
The report names each row after what it holds and the sample it belongs to. These are the names, the files they come from and the modes that have them:

Row From Modes fastp read QC | <sample> 01.reads/{sample}/illumina/{sample}_fastp.json illumina, hybrid NanoPlot raw read QC | <sample>, NanoPlot filtered read QC | <sample> 01.reads/{sample}/long/raw_qc/{sample}_NanoStats.txt, filtered_qc/{sample}_NanoStats.txt longread, hybrid mapping QC | <sample> 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/qualimap/: the sample's reads on the draft illumina, longread, hybrid mapping Illumina QC | <sample> 02.assembly/{sample}/guide/eval/qualimap/: the Illumina pairs on the guide hybrid QUAST guide assembly QC | <sample> eval/quast/report.tsv, the row labelled {sample}_guide hybrid QUAST assembly QC | <sample> eval/quast/report.tsv all BUSCO completeness QC (<lineage>) | <sample> eval/busco/short_summary.generic.<lineage>.{sample}.txt or short_summary.specific.<lineage>.{sample}.txt all <sample>: <contig> eval/contig_summary_mqc.tsv, one row per contig of the draft assembly all <sample>: <target> 05.amr/{sample}/amr_summary_mqc.tsv, one row per target protein all, AMR screen on

These names were checked in finished runs of the three read-based modes on one public genome, and of longread and hybrid with PacBio HiFi reads on a second. The runs are described on Validation on public genomes. A row whose name does not come out as above shows the raw folder path instead. Its numbers are not affected.

With parameters.busco.lineage: auto, BUSCO writes a generic summary, for the broad lineage it tried first, and a specific one, for the lineage it ended with. Every sample then gets two BUSCO rows. With a named lineage, it gets one.

Sample names are shown in full. Otherwise MultiQC would cut a name at the first file ending it knows, such as .clean or .sorted. A sample named SAMPLE1.clean would then get a wrong name, and two such samples would share one row. The names do not depend on where the output folder lies.

docs.title: What the report shows
docs.text:
For QUAST and BUSCO, the General Statistics table of the report shows by default the N50, the assembly length and the complete single-copy and missing BUSCO counts. Its numbers are in 06.report/multiqc_data/multiqc_general_stats.txt. That file has one line for each row name listed above except the contig-summary and AMR rows, for example QUAST assembly QC | SAMPLE1. Each line fills only the columns of its own tool. The QUAST and BUSCO columns are these:

Column Unit In the General Statistics table of the report quast-N50 kb shown quast-Total_length Mb shown, as the assembly length busco-complete BUSCO genes hidden by default busco-complete_single_copy BUSCO genes shown busco-complete_duplicated BUSCO genes hidden by default busco-fragmented BUSCO genes hidden by default busco-missing BUSCO genes shown

The complete, duplicated and fragmented counts can be switched on in the column settings of the General Statistics table.

The sections of the report for QUAST, BUSCO and the two FunFlux tables hold the following:

Section of the report What it holds QUAST the full QUAST table and a plot of contig counts by length BUSCO one bar chart per dataset Contig summary contig_summary_mqc.tsv of every sample as one table, one row per contig of the draft assembly with all 20 columns of the file; the table's column settings show or hide columns, and multiqc_data/multiqc_contig_summary.txt holds the numbers. It is not part of the General Statistics table AMR mutations (ChroQueTas), with the AMR screen on amr_summary_mqc.tsv of every sample as one table, one row per target protein of the species: its status, the positions compared, the verdict, the FungAMR mutations and new mutations found, and the drugs with evidence of resistance and of no resistance, with their levels (The tables)

MultiQC shows a table with more than 500 rows as a violin plot

The limit is MultiQC's max_table_rows setting. The contig summary has one row per contig of every sample, so for a batch of fragmented assemblies, read 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/contig_summary.tsv itself, as described under Contig summary.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Rule multiqc writes the report, the configuration it was made with, the numbers behind it and a log:

Path Content 06.report/multiqc_report.html the report 06.report/multiqc_config.yaml the configuration the report was made with: no absolute paths and no creation date and time at the top of the page (show_analysis_paths: False, show_analysis_time: False), sample names not shortened (fn_clean_sample_names: false), and the rules that turn folder paths into the sample names above (sample_names_replace) 06.report/multiqc_data/ the numbers behind the page as text and JSON: multiqc_general_stats.txt (one line per row name of the report), multiqc_quast.txt, multiqc_busco.txt, multiqc_contig_summary.txt, multiqc_data.json, MultiQC's own multiqc.log, and more logs/multiqc.log what MultiQC printed

The report covers the samples of the current run only and is made again when they change. multiqc_data/ is then replaced as a whole.

To combine several runs in one report, run MultiQC yourself with --ignore '*/busco/run_*' --ignore '*/busco/auto_lineage'. The kept BUSCO folders hold extra copies of each BUSCO summary, and without these two options each copy shows as one more BUSCO row.

A personal MultiQC configuration cannot move the report or multiqc_data/, because multiqc_config.yaml sets their names and is read last.

docs.title: Choosing a mode
docs.text:
Choose the mode from the data you have: Illumina paired-end reads, ONT or PacBio HiFi reads, both kinds of reads for the same isolates, or an existing assembly. This page shows which mode fits which data, how to name the input files, and what happens when the mode or a file name is wrong.

The mode key selects the front end, the steps that differ between modes. These are read processing, assembly and the contig filter before the contamination and mitochondrion screen, and polishing after it. From the screen on, every mode runs the same steps except polishing, which differs between the read-based modes.

Terms used on this page

front end the steps that differ by mode, chosen by mode: read processing, assembly and contig filter before the screen, and polishing after it the screen the contamination and mitochondrion screen: BLAST against core_nt, BlobTools, the mitochondrion screen and the contig selector; in contigs mode only with parameters.contigs.screen: true batch the samples one run finds in the input folders of its mode; files of one kind share one extension guide assembly in hybrid, the SPAdes assembly of the Illumina reads; it is screened, and only the pairs that map to it go on dry run a Snakemake run with -n: FunFlux checks the configuration and the inputs, and Snakemake lists the jobs it plans without running any; it takes seconds NOTE a line starting [FunFlux] NOTE that reports something to check without stopping the run; read them after every dry run nuclear genome the delivered genome without the confirmed mitochondrial contigs, contigs_final.fasta; it holds every contig when nothing is split off (no screen, or parameters.mitochondria.mode off or report)

docs.title: Which mode for which data
docs.text:
Each kind of data has its own mode, input key and file-name convention, and the input files must follow that convention.

Your data mode Input key File names Illumina paired-end reads illumina input.illumina_dir {sample}_R1.<ext> and {sample}_R2.<ext> ONT reads, PacBio HiFi reads, or a batch with both longread input.longread_dir {sample}_ont.<ext> or {sample}_pacbio.<ext> Illumina pairs plus ONT or PacBio HiFi reads of the same isolates hybrid input.illumina_dir and input.longread_dir (may be the same folder) both conventions, every sample on both sides An assembly in FASTA format contigs input.contigs_dir {sample}.fasta, {sample}.fa or {sample}.fna Some isolates with Illumina reads only, others with ONT or PacBio HiFi reads only one run per mode: illumina for the first group, longread for the second, each with its own configuration file each run its own input folder as in those rows

<ext> is fastq, fq, fastq.gz or fq.gz. Only the input key of the active mode is read, and the others may stay empty. Isolates with different kinds of data go into separate runs, as the last row shows. These runs may share one output_dir and one annotation parameter table when their sample names differ, as described in Running several batches.

The modes differ in the steps below, and the Modes pages describe each mode in detail.

illumina longread hybrid contigs Reads PhiX removal (bowtie2), adapter and quality trimming (fastp) Filtlong; NanoPlot before and after both; Filtlong as in longread, optionally guided by the Illumina pairs none Assembly SPAdes --isolate; contigs of at least 500 bp and 2x coverage kept hifiasm (default) or Flye SPAdes guide assembly of the Illumina reads, then hifiasm or Flye of the long reads your FASTA (below) Polishing none Medaka, ONT samples only Medaka for ONT samples, then Polypolish with the Illumina reads none Mitochondrion found by BLAST found by BLAST, supported by read depth or circularity from the assembler; a BLAST hit covering at least 70 % confirms alone as longread; the guide assembly is screened as well only with parameters.contigs.screen: true, by BLAST

contigs mode starts from a finished assembly and has no read steps. hybrid does the most work, because it assembles twice. The Illumina reads build a guide assembly whose screen selects the isolate's read pairs, and Polypolish corrects the final long-read assembly with these selected pairs. If you switch on the optional Filtlong guidance, the same pairs also score the ONT reads. hybrid needs both read types for every sample.

docs.title: File names
docs.text:
FunFlux finds the samples from their file names. A file that breaks its mode's convention stops the run or is not found, so check the names before the first run.

Item Accepted Not accepted Sample name the part of the file name before _R1/_R2, _ont/_pacbio, or, in contigs mode, before the last dot: SAMPLE1_R1.fastq.gz is sample SAMPLE1, my.genome.fasta is sample my.genome; underscores and dots are allowed a space or one of the characters listed below the table stops the run Extension one extension for all files of one kind in a batch a folder with both .fastq.gz and .fq.gz reads stops the run (more than one file extension in this folder) Illumina reads paired: one R1 and one R2 file per sample, and the name must end in _R1.<ext>; concatenate the files of several lanes or runs first an R1 file without its R2 stops the run; a name with more after _R1, such as SAMPLE1_S1_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz, is not found, so rename or link the files Long reads one file per sample an _ont and a _pacbio file for the same sample stop the run contigs FASTA uncompressed FASTA only .fasta.gz stops the run; every file in the folder whose name contains a dot is read as a sample, so a README.txt there stops the run as well

The characters that stop the run in a sample name are a space and any of * # @ % ^ / ! ? & : ; | < >.

The sample name also becomes the locus-tag prefix of every gene that funannotate writes. NCBI accepts a locus-tag prefix of 3 to 12 letters or digits that starts with a letter. A sample name that does not fit still runs, and a NOTE then says that the gene IDs cannot be submitted to GenBank as they are. Every sample needs a line in the annotation parameter table.

docs.title: Mixing ONT and PacBio HiFi samples
docs.text:
In longread and hybrid mode, the file-name suffix sets the technology of each sample. {sample}_ont.<ext> is Oxford Nanopore and {sample}_pacbio.<ext> is PacBio HiFi (CCS). One batch may hold both, but one sample must not have both files. Some settings are chosen once for the whole run, and others for each sample.

Setting Chosen The assembler (parameters.<mode>.assembler) once for the whole run The Filtlong settings once for the whole run, for both technologies; their defaults are sized for ONT reads The assembler's flags, the minimap2 preset, Medaka and, in hybrid, the Filtlong guidance when it is on per sample, from the suffix; the dry run prints the decision for every sample (One technology per sample) Everything after polishing (contigs_all.fasta) the same for both technologies

One batch can therefore mix the two technologies, and only the steps up to polishing treat them differently. In hybrid, PacBio samples get Filtlong's plain length and quality filter and no Medaka, and Polypolish still corrects them with the Illumina reads.

docs.title: PacBio CLR reads are not supported
docs.text:
_pacbio means HiFi (CCS) reads, and no step is set up for continuous long reads (CLR). For a _pacbio sample, hifiasm runs in its HiFi mode, Flye gets --pacbio-hifi, minimap2 gets map-hifi, and Medaka is skipped. FunFlux does not measure read accuracy, so a _pacbio file of CLR reads is assembled with these settings without an error. The only message is the NOTE of every dry run with _pacbio samples:

[FunFlux] NOTE: samples with a _pacbio file are assumed to hold PacBio HiFi (CCS) reads: GXU8616. Continuous long reads (CLR) are not supported by this workflow.

docs.title: Contigs from another assembler
docs.text:
In contigs mode, the contig filter looks at the first header of each FASTA, and only a FASTA with SPAdes headers loses contigs at this step.

First header Contigs removed Headers SPAdes (>NODE_<n>_length_<L>_cov_<C>) shorter than 500 bp or with a coverage below 2, as in illumina mode stay as they are Any other (Flye, hifiasm, a sequencing provider, a database download) none cut at the first space or tab

logs/filter_contigs_{sample}.log names the branch taken and reports Kept N of M records., and the run stops when no contig is left.

Later, before gene prediction, funannotate clean removes contigs shorter than 500 bp and duplicated contigs shorter than the N50, such as duplicated haplotypes in a provider assembly. Its rules are given on Repeat masking. 04.annotation/{sample}/contigs_removed_by_clean.txt lists the removed contigs, while QUAST, BUSCO and the ITS steps still see every contig of contigs_final.fasta.

docs.title: When to switch on the screen in contigs mode
docs.text:
In contigs mode the screen runs only with parameters.contigs.screen: true, and it then needs directories.blast_db, the folder that holds NCBI core_nt:

directories:
  blast_db: /path/to/NCBI_core_nt

parameters:
  contigs:
    screen: true

The screen searches every contig with BLAST against NCBI core_nt, assigns it a genus with BlobTools and tests it for a match to a mitochondrial genome. With the default parameters.mitochondria.mode: separate_confirmed, the screen moves confirmed mitochondrial contigs to 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_mitochondrial.fasta. contigs_final.fasta is then the nuclear genome, and contigs_all.fasta holds both.

Switch the screen on when the FASTA may hold a mitochondrion or you want to look for contamination, and core_nt is at hand.

Screen When on The assembly may contain the mitochondrial genome; an assembly from a sequencing provider usually does. Without the screen it is annotated with the nuclear gene predictor, although fungal mitochondria use a different genetic code (code 4 in most fungi, code 3 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and related yeasts). on You want a BLAST taxonomy per contig to look for contamination: 02.assembly/{sample}/contaminants/contig_taxonomy_decisions.tsv has a line per contig and {sample}_composition.txt the share of each genus. off The FASTA is already a nuclear genome, for example the contigs_final.fasta of an earlier FunFlux run that split the mitochondrion off. off core_nt is not available: the screen needs directories.blast_db with core_nt, taxdb.btd, taxdb.bti, nodes.dmp and names.dmp.

With the default parameters.decontamination.mode: off, the screen removes no contig and only splits off the confirmed mitochondrion. The screen adds 8 jobs per sample.

Without reads, the contigs are mapped against themselves only because BlobTools needs a BAM file. That coverage carries no information, and a contig is confirmed as mitochondrial by BLAST alone, when a mitochondrial genome covers at least min_direct_blast_qcov (35 %) of it. See Decontamination and Mitochondria.

docs.title: What a wrong mode does
docs.text:
The four file-name conventions do not overlap, so most wrong modes and folders stop the dry run. The checks run in a fixed order and stop at the first problem.

A wrong mode value:

[FunFlux] mode: must be one of illumina | longread | hybrid | contigs (got: 'ilumina')

The input key of the mode is not set, or is not a folder:

[FunFlux] mode=illumina requires input.illumina_dir to be set in the config.
[FunFlux] input.illumina_dir: '/path/to/reads' is not an existing directory.

illumina on long reads, or on files named _R1_001.fastq.gz:

[FunFlux] input.illumina_dir: no input files found. Expected names like {sample}_R1.fastq.gz and {sample}_R2.fastq.gz.

longread on Illumina reads:

[FunFlux] input.longread_dir: no input files found. Expected names like {sample}_ont.fastq.gz or {sample}_pacbio.fastq.gz.

contigs on a folder of reads, or on compressed FASTA:

[FunFlux] input.contigs_dir: file extension 'gz' is not recognised (expected one of: fasta, fa, fna).

hybrid with a sample that has reads of one kind only:

[FunFlux] hybrid mode needs Illumina and long reads for every sample.
  No _ont or _pacbio file for: GXU8616

A sample with both long-read suffixes:

[FunFlux] sample 'SAMPLE1' has both _ont and _pacbio files in /path/to/reads. Provide one long-read technology per sample.

Without directories.blast_db, a run with the screen (every read-based mode, and contigs mode with the screen on) stops before the input folder is read:

[FunFlux] directories.blast_db: required, but it is missing or empty in the config.

Three wrong choices do not stop the run

  • illumina or longread on a folder that holds both kinds of reads runs with the files of its own convention and ignores the others. If both belong to the same isolates, the mode is hybrid.
  • contigs without the screen annotates a mitochondrial genome in the FASTA as nuclear. The NOTE printed on every such run says so.
  • CLR reads named _pacbio are assembled with HiFi settings.

docs.title: Reference databases
docs.text:
FunFlux needs reference databases in addition to its conda environments. You provide three of them before the first run: NCBI core_nt with its taxonomy files (not read in contigs mode without the screen), the eggNOG-mapper data and InterProScan. The workflow, BUSCO and Medaka fetch the rest, on the computer that runs Snakemake, except BUSCO with auto, which downloads inside each job. snakemake download_all fetches all of it in advance, except BUSCO's data with auto, as described in Preparation, on a computer with internet.

The table lists every database with its configuration key, when that key is required, who provides the data, its version and its size.

Database Config key Key required Provided by Version Size NCBI core_nt and taxonomy files directories.blast_db; parameters.nt_version names the database with the contamination and mitochondrion screen: illumina, longread, hybrid, and contigs with parameters.contigs.screen: true you NCBI's current build; tested with the build of 11 July 2026 264 GB eggNOG-mapper data directories.eggnog_db yes you eggNOG 5.0.2 48 GB InterProScan member databases files.iprscan yes you, with InterProScan 5.78-109.0 7.0 GB download, 50 GB installed funannotate database directories.funannotate_db, links.funannotate_link yes the workflow, when the folder holds no database funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08 2.1 GB archive; 6.1 GB unpacked, 8.1 GB with the archive UNITE links.unite_its_link, or directories.unite_db the link, unless directories.unite_db is set the workflow, once per output folder; or your copy UNITE release for eukaryotes, 19.02.2025 35.7 MB download, 207 MB unpacked antiSMASH databases directories.antismash_db no the workflow, once per output folder; or your copy as downloaded by antiSMASH 8.0.4 9.4 GB Tiberius model links.tiberius_model_link, parameters.tiberius.model_sha256 the link, unless parameters.tiberius.mode is off the workflow, once per output folder the fungi model of 8 February 2026 30 MB download, 31 MB unpacked Telomere repeat database links.telomere_db_link, parameters.contig_summary.telomere_db_sha256 yes the workflow, once per output folder telo_database_v2.tsv of tidk, at the commit the template link names 0.6 MB ChroQueTas and the FungAMR database links.chroquetas_link, parameters.amr.chroquetas_script_sha256, parameters.amr.chroquetas_db_sha256 only with parameters.amr.chroquetas: on (off by default) the workflow, once per output folder ChroQueTas 1.0.1 and its database db-v20250811 (57 species) 29 kB script, 137 kB archive; 2.5 MB unpacked BUSCO lineage datasets parameters.busco.lineage no (default auto) BUSCO, in every BUSCO job with auto; the workflow, once per output folder, for a named lineage odb12 per archive, e.g. eukaryota_odb12 29 MB, hypocreales_odb12 275 MB PhiX genome links.phix_link in illumina and hybrid the workflow, once per output folder (download_phix) GCF_000819615.1 2 kB Medaka model parameters.longread.medaka_model, parameters.hybrid.medaka_model no (default auto) Medaka, during the model check, the first time a model is used named, or worked out from the reads not measured

Sizes on disk are as du -h prints them, in powers of 1024. Download and archive sizes are the byte counts the servers list, in decimal units. The databases you keep yourself take about 380 GB with a local antiSMASH copy, and 264 GB of that is core_nt, which only the screen reads.

Terms used on this page

taxonomy files the files taxdb.btd and taxdb.bti, which give BLAST its organism names, and nodes.dmp and names.dmp, the NCBI taxonomy BlobTools reads; all beside core_nt NOTE a line starting [FunFlux] NOTE that reports something to check without stopping the run; read them after every dry run funannotate database the frozen snapshot of funannotate's data, such as Swiss-Prot, Pfam, the BUSCO set and stored AUGUSTUS models, downloaded once from Zenodo into directories.funannotate_db stored AUGUSTUS model the AUGUSTUS parameters trained earlier for one species, kept in trained_species/ of the funannotate database; named in column 4 of the annotation parameter table, they are used as they are path repair rule normalize_funannotate_db: it rewrites the absolute paths stored in the funannotate database to your folder, in place and without a lock, so start one run first launch folder the folder Snakemake is started from, normally the FunFlux repository; relative paths are read from it, and .snakemake/ is created there BUSCO set the BUSCO genes funannotate looks for to train SNAP, GlimmerHMM and, without a stored AUGUSTUS model, AUGUSTUS: dikarya (dikarya_odb9) unless parameters.prediction.busco_db names another lineage dataset the BUSCO gene set of one taxonomic group, such as hypocreales_odb12, for the completeness check; with lineage: auto, BUSCO chooses one by placing the genome

docs.title: NCBI core_nt and taxonomy files
docs.text:
The contamination and mitochondrion screen searches every contig against this database with blastn -task megablast (rule blast_contigs). BlobTools reads the NCBI taxonomy from the same folder (rule blob_json), so directories.blast_db must hold three kinds of files:

Files From Used for core_nt.nal, core_nt.00.*, core_nt.01.*, ... update_blastdb.pl core_nt the search; parameters.nt_version (default core_nt) is the database name taxdb.btd, taxdb.bti taxdb.tar.gz organism names in the BLAST table; without them the name columns read N/A nodes.dmp, names.dmp taxdump.tar.gz the taxonomy tree and names BlobTools uses to assign a taxon to each contig

parameters.nt_version: nt selects the full nt database instead, if that is what the folder holds. These commands download core_nt and the taxonomy files:

conda create -n blast -c conda-forge -c bioconda blast=2.16.0   # provides update_blastdb.pl
conda activate blast
mkdir -p /path/to/blast_db && cd /path/to/blast_db
update_blastdb.pl --decompress --num_threads 4 core_nt
wget -c https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/blast/db/taxdb.tar.gz && tar -zxf taxdb.tar.gz
wget -c https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pub/taxonomy/taxdump.tar.gz && tar -zxf taxdump.tar.gz

update_blastdb.pl checks every archive against the .md5 file NCBI publishes beside it, and --decompress unpacks each archive and deletes it. The build of 11 July 2026 has 80 volumes (252 GB) and 12 GB of database-wide index files, and the taxonomy files add 0.8 GB. FunFlux v2 does not read nucl_gb.accession2taxid (13 GB), which the v1 instructions also downloaded.

Two commands check the database and the taxonomy files:

BLASTDB=/path/to/blast_db blastdbcmd -db core_nt -info | head -4
ls /path/to/blast_db/taxdb.btd /path/to/blast_db/taxdb.bti /path/to/blast_db/nodes.dmp /path/to/blast_db/names.dmp

For the build of 11 July 2026, the first command prints:

Database: Core nucleotide BLAST database
    128,460,233 sequences; 947,384,893,387 total bases

Date: Jul 11, 2026  1:17 AM Longest sequence: 98,200,793 bases

A dry run that passes does not show that the volumes and taxdb are in place

A missing folder is noticed before any job starts, with a NOTE. A missing nodes.dmp or names.dmp is noticed in a dry run with the screen on, which stops with MissingInputException in rule blob_json because both files are inputs of blob_json. Missing volumes or a missing taxdb are noticed only when BLAST runs, which first reads them.

docs.title: eggNOG-mapper data
docs.text:
FunFlux runs eggNOG-mapper 2.1.13, which reads the data of eggNOG 5.0.2. The data for eggnog-mapper 3.x (eggNOG 7) do not work with it, so download the data with eggNOG-mapper 2.1.13 itself:

conda create -n eggnog-mapper -c conda-forge -c bioconda eggnog-mapper=2.1.13
conda activate eggnog-mapper
mkdir -p /path/to/eggnog_db
download_eggnog_data.py --data_dir /path/to/eggnog_db -y

The script fetches eggnog.db, eggnog.taxa.db and the DIAMOND database eggnog_proteins.dmnd from eggnogdb.embl.de with wget, which the environment contains, and -y answers its questions with yes. The Pfam, MMseqs2 and HMMER databases are downloaded only on request (-P, -M, -H). FunFlux does not use them, because it runs emapper.py -m diamond.

To check the download, list the folder:

ls -lh /path/to/eggnog_db
# eggnog.db 39G, eggnog_proteins.dmnd 8.7G, eggnog.taxa.db 266M, eggnog.taxa.db.traverse.pkl 6.4M

FunFlux prints a NOTE before any job starts when the folder does not exist. The files themselves are first read when eggnog_annotation runs, after gene prediction.

docs.title: funannotate database snapshot
docs.text:
funannotate needs its own database. FunFlux does not build one with funannotate setup but takes a frozen snapshot from Zenodo, funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08, record 23265189 (10.5281/zenodo.23265189). It was written on 8 October 2026 by funannotate setup -i all -b dikarya --wget with funannotate 1.8.17, the version FunFlux runs. All versions of the funannotate database on Zenodo share the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18271294, which leads to the newest.

The database holds the components below, with the versions to cite for the annotation databases. Most of these versions are those funannotate wrote into the database index. The dikarya_odb9 row comes from the description file of that BUSCO set, and the row of the stored AUGUSTUS models from the AUGUSTUS version that built the database. The Zenodo record also holds the versions as a table, funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08.versions.tsv.

Component Version Records UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot 2026_03 575,748 Pfam 38.2 30,134 InterPro 110.0 54,922 Gene Ontology 2026-07-26 48,340 gene2product 1.99 34,505 dbCAN HMMdb V11 (funannotate's index calls it 14.0) 699 MEROPS 12.5 (the label funannotate 1.8.17 gives it) 5,098 MIBiG 1.4 31,023 repeat proteins 1.0 11,950 BUSCO outgroups 1.0 8 in the index; outgroups/ holds the sets of 6 species BUSCO dikarya_odb9 2016-02-13 1,312 BUSCOs stored AUGUSTUS models, in trained_species/ (AUGUSTUS and other gene-finder parameters) from AUGUSTUS 3.5.0 166 Five databases are newer than in the previous snapshot (FunFlux v1)

The previous snapshot, funannotate_db_1.8.15_2025-12-15 (record 18271295, named for funannotate 1.8.15), stays on Zenodo, and FunFlux v1 downloads it. A folder that already holds it keeps it. To use the new snapshot, point directories.funannotate_db at a new, empty folder, for the reasons given under Newer snapshots.

Component Previous snapshot (2025-12-15) UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot 2025_04, 573,661 records Pfam 38.0, 25,545 records InterPro 107.0, 49,674 records Gene Ontology 2025-10-10, 48,196 records gene2product 1.97, 34,471 records MEROPS the same file, labelled 12.0 dbCAN, MIBiG, repeat proteins, BUSCO outgroups, BUSCO dikarya_odb9, stored AUGUSTUS models the same

The other components hold the same data. Because five databases are newer, the gene names, products, domains and GO terms of a new annotation can differ from those made with the previous snapshot. The gene models can differ too, because funannotate predict also aligns Swiss-Prot to the genome as protein evidence.

docs.title: What the workflow does
docs.text:
Two steps prepare the funannotate database. It is downloaded once per database folder, and the path repair checks its stored paths in every new output folder.

Step (name in the log) When What it does funannotate_db only while <funannotate_db>/funannotate-db-info.txt is missing downloads the archive named by links.funannotate_link and its .sha256 file from the same Zenodo record, checks the archive with sha256sum -c and unpacks it into the folder; archive and checksum file stay there. Log: logs/funannotate_db.log normalize_funannotate_db in every new output folder the funannotate database stores absolute paths in funannotate-db-info.txt and trained_species/*/info.json; the step rewrites those that do not point into your folder and leaves correct files alone. Summary: 00.resources/funannotate_db_paths.normalized.json

A checksum mismatch stops the run with [FunFlux] funannotate_db: ... does not match its checksum file ..., so it was NOT unpacked. Delete both files, the archive and its checksum file, and run again.

One run at a time until the paths are repaired

normalize_funannotate_db rewrites files inside the database folder, in place and without a lock. Two runs that start at the same time on a database whose paths are not yet repaired can damage it. Start one run and let it pass this step before you start the others on the same folder. Once the paths are repaired, the step only reads the database. Keep the folder writable until then.

Reach the folder under the same real path in every run. A run that sees it under another path, as a second user or a second machine may, rewrites the stored paths. funannotate-db-info.txt then changes, and the next run on any other output folder repeats the repair and every annotation step after it.

docs.title: Downloading it by hand
docs.text:
For a machine without internet access at run time, these commands take the same steps as rule funannotate_db:

mkdir -p /path/to/funannotate_db && cd /path/to/funannotate_db
curl -L --fail -o funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08.tar.gz \
    'https://zenodo.org/records/23265189/files/funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08.tar.gz?download=1'
curl -L --fail -o funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08.sha256 \
    'https://zenodo.org/records/23265189/files/funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08.sha256?download=1'
sha256sum -c funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08.sha256   # funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08.tar.gz: OK
tar -xzf funannotate_db_1.8.17_2026-10-08.tar.gz --strip-components=1
ls funannotate-db-info.txt dikarya trained_species

docs.title: Using the snapshot without FunFlux
docs.text:
The funannotate database also serves funannotate 1.8.17 on its own, once its stored paths are rewritten the way normalize_funannotate_db does it:

mkdir -p /path/to/funannotate_db
tar -xzf funannotate_db_<version>_<date>.tar.gz --strip-components=1 -C /path/to/funannotate_db
cd /path/to/funannotate_db
OLD=$(head -n 1 funannotate-db-info.txt | cut -f 3 | xargs dirname)
sed -i "s#${OLD}#$(pwd)#g" funannotate-db-info.txt trained_species/*/info.json
export FUNANNOTATE_DB=/path/to/funannotate_db
funannotate database

The sed line reads the stored prefix from the database index and replaces it with the current folder, in the index and in the info.json of every stored AUGUSTUS model. The folder's path must not contain & or #, which sed would read as instructions. The last command should list ten databases.

docs.title: Newer snapshots, and building your own
docs.text:
Which snapshot a run uses depends on what the folder directories.funannotate_db holds:

The folder What FunFlux does is empty, or has no funannotate-db-info.txt downloads the snapshot links.funannotate_link names holds a funannotate database uses it, whatever links.funannotate_link names holds a funannotate database that an earlier run from the same launch folder downloaded, and links.funannotate_link has changed since unpacks the new archive over the old files and leaves behind those the new one does not replace (What makes Snakemake re-run a rule)

For a new snapshot, point directories.funannotate_db at a new, empty folder

As the table shows, a folder that already holds a funannotate database either keeps it or has the new archive unpacked over its old files. Other runs and workflows may also still read the old folder.

To build a database with the current UniProt, Pfam, InterPro and Gene Ontology releases yourself, run miscellaneous/build_funannotate_db.sh in FunFlux's funannotate environment:

conda activate /path/to/the/funannotate/environment    # the folder --list-conda-envs prints
bash miscellaneous/build_funannotate_db.sh /path/to/funannotate_db_build dikarya
  • Activate the environment with conda activate. With only its bin/ folder on the PATH, the setup misses AUGUSTUS_CONFIG_PATH, which activation sets. The script stops with a message when that variable is not set, or when funannotate is missing or not version 1.8.17.
  • The script needs network access and about 9 GB of free space in the folder named as its first argument, and takes about 10 minutes. It refuses to overwrite a database folder, archive or checksum file that already exists.
  • It runs funannotate setup -i all -b <BUSCO sets> -d <folder> --wget and checks that the ten databases, the BUSCO sets and the stored AUGUSTUS models all arrived. It writes the database folder funannotate_db_<YYYY.MM.DD>/ and an archive of it, funannotate_db_<funannotate version>_<date>.tar.gz, with its .sha256 file. It also writes a table of the database versions (.versions.tsv) and two logs.
  • Point directories.funannotate_db at the database folder it wrote. That folder holds funannotate-db-info.txt, so nothing is downloaded.
  • The script ends by printing the steps to publish the archive on Zenodo. For your own runs you need none of them: keep the database folder and point directories.funannotate_db at it.

docs.title: Other BUSCO sets for gene prediction
docs.text:
funannotate predict trains SNAP and GlimmerHMM on the conserved genes of the BUSCO set named by parameters.prediction.busco_db. It trains AUGUSTUS on them too, for the samples without a model in column 4 of the annotation parameter table.

Set BUSCO genes In the funannotate database Tested with FunFlux v2 dikarya, the default 1,312 yes, the only one yes fungi 290 no no: its download has not been tested

Keep dikarya unless the fungus lies outside the Dikarya. AUGUSTUS needs at least 200 genes to train on, so with fungi a sample is safer with a stored AUGUSTUS model in column 4. When a funannotate database is present and the named set is not, every Snakemake command stops before any job starts and prints the command that adds the set, funannotate setup -i busco -b <set> -d <folder> -w. Run it in FunFlux's funannotate environment, activated as below.

For a fungus outside the Dikarya (Ascomycota and Basidiomycota), add a set such as fungi with funannotate 1.8.17, for example from the environment FunFlux built. Run the first command while busco_db is still dikarya, with the --conda-prefix of your runs, or without it if you use none:

snakemake --sdm conda --list-conda-envs --conda-prefix /path/to/funflux_envs \
    --configfile config/config_custom.yaml          # prints the folder of funannotate.yaml
conda activate /path/to/that/folder
funannotate setup -i busco -b fungi -d /path/to/funannotate_db -w

If the folder does not exist yet, build the environments first, as described in Building the environments in advance. Then set parameters.prediction.busco_db: fungi.

  • Activate the environment with conda activate. With only its bin/ folder on the PATH, setup stops with KeyError: 'AUGUSTUS_CONFIG_PATH'.
  • -i busco limits the downloads to BUSCO sets. Setup still copies into trained_species/ the AUGUSTUS species files the database lacks (it already holds all 166), rewrites funannotate-db-info.txt from the lines it can read, and writes funannotate-setup.log into the current folder.
  • -w makes funannotate download with wget instead of its own downloader, which has failed on some of funannotate's download links: an HTTP 308 redirect on the dikarya link, and HTTP 403 from geneontology.org.

Adding a set this way has been tried only with the small microsporidia set. The fungi download has not been tested, and FunFlux v2 was tested with dikarya only.

docs.title: UNITE
docs.text:
FunFlux classifies the ITS1 and ITS2 sequences with vsearch --sintax against UNITE. The default links.unite_its_link is the UNITE USEARCH/UTAX/SINTAX release for eukaryotes, version 19.02.2025 (DOI 10.15156/BIO/3301246), which covers all eukaryotes, not Fungi only. FunFlux either downloads this file or links your local copy:

Default: download Local copy: directories.unite_db Rule unite_db unite_db_local What it does streams the file through gzip -dc into 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.fasta, once per output folder links the file into 00.resources/unite/ 00.resources/unite/PROVENANCE.txt records the link, the download date, the md5 and the size the folder, the date, the md5 and the size Check no checksum is verified the run stops before any job starts when the folder holds no uncompressed unite_its_sintax.fasta

A local copy serves any number of output folders. To make one, download and unpack the file yourself:

mkdir -p /path/to/unite && cd /path/to/unite
curl -L --fail 'https://s3.hpc.ut.ee/plutof-public/original/338a1413-6039-4e00-b5cf-410346a1e366.gz' \
    | gzip -dc > unite_its_sintax.fasta
grep -c '^>' unite_its_sintax.fasta   # 266589
md5sum unite_its_sintax.fasta         # 4cacdc7f2372e0d1e863d7f9715a5843

directories:
  unite_db: /path/to/unite

When links.unite_its_link is also set, a NOTE says that it is not used. Another UNITE release in USEARCH/UTAX/SINTAX format can replace the default through either key, and its classifications can then differ from those of the default release.

Downloaded or linked, the file is then filtered. Rule unite_identified keeps the records whose taxonomy names a genus in 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.identified.fasta, and SINTAX reads that file unless parameters.its.unite_identified_only is false. See The UNITE reference filter.

docs.title: antiSMASH databases
docs.text:
The antiSMASH databases end up in 00.resources/antismash/databases/ of the output folder, either downloaded there or linked from a copy you hold:

Default: download Local copy: directories.antismash_db Rule antismash_db antismash_db_local What it does runs download-antismash-databases of antiSMASH 8.0.4 into 00.resources/antismash/databases/, once per output folder, from dl.secondarymetabolites.org and ftp.ebi.ac.uk (Pfam 35.0); the folder, 9.4 GB, stays for later runs in the same output folder fills 00.resources/antismash/databases/ with one symbolic link per entry of your folder; nothing is copied, and FunFlux does not write into your folder

A local copy saves 9.4 GB in every output folder and serves any number of them. To make one:

conda create -n antismash -c conda-forge -c bioconda antismash=8.0.4
conda activate antismash
download-antismash-databases --database-dir /path/to/antismash_db
ls /path/to/antismash_db
# as-js  clusterblast  clustercompare  comparippson  knownclusterblast  mite  nrps_pks  pfam  resfam  tigrfam

The downloader ends with Pre-building all databases... and done.. Use a database made by antiSMASH 8.0.4, the version FunFlux runs.

directories:
  antismash_db: /path/to/antismash_db

The run stops before any job starts when the folder does not exist or has no clusterblast/. Otherwise FunFlux prints Using the local antiSMASH database at '/path/to/antismash_db'. Nothing will be downloaded.

docs.title: BUSCO lineage datasets
docs.text:
There is nothing to download beforehand. Where BUSCO 6.0.0 gets its lineage data from busco-data.ezlab.org depends on the setting:

parameters.busco.lineage BUSCO option Downloaded Where and when auto (default) --auto-lineage-euk eukaryota_odb12 (29 MB), the eukaryote placement files (8 MB) and the lineage BUSCO places the genome in by every BUSCO job, into 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/busco/busco_tmp, which Snakemake deletes when the job ends. Samples never share a download, because BUSCO 6.0.0 has no lock on its download folder and silently updates a shared one a lineage name, e.g. hypocreales_odb12 -l hypocreales_odb12 --offline that dataset once per output folder, by rule busco_data, into 00.resources/busco/, on the computer that runs Snakemake; every BUSCO job reads it there

With auto, every BUSCO job needs network access

A named lineage needs network access once, and the downloaded dataset stays at the version in 00.resources/busco/ for later runs into the same output folder. BUSCO fetches the newest version of a dataset, so with auto completeness can also shift when a new version is published.

busco --list-datasets in a BUSCO 6.0.0 environment lists the names, each with its version after a dot, such as hypocreales_odb12.2. Write the name without the dot and the number after it: hypocreales_odb12.

The BUSCO set that funannotate trains its gene finders on (parameters.prediction.busco_db, dikarya_odb9) is a different dataset. It is part of the funannotate database, as described under Other BUSCO sets for gene prediction.

docs.title: Tiberius model
docs.text:
The gene finder Tiberius, on by default, needs the fungi model its authors trained, a set of network weights. Rule tiberius_model downloads it from links.tiberius_model_link, on the Tiberius authors' server, once per output folder. It checks the archive against parameters.tiberius.model_sha256 with sha256sum -c and unpacks it into 00.resources/tiberius/model/ (model_config.json, model_layers.json, weights.h5). FunFlux does not ship or mirror the model, because no licence is published with it.

The address carries no version number. When the authors replace the model there, the checksum no longer matches, the run stops before anything is unpacked, and the downloaded file is kept as 00.resources/tiberius/model.tar.gz. Either set parameters.tiberius.mode: off, or check the new model and accept it:

sha256sum /path/to/output_dir/00.resources/tiberius/model.tar.gz
# put the 64 characters it prints into parameters.tiberius.model_sha256, then run again

A new checksum re-runs Tiberius for every sample, and the gene prediction after it.

docs.title: Telomere repeat database
docs.text:
The contig summary chooses the telomere repeat unit of every assembly from the data and checks the units it weighs against the database that comes with tidk (Brown et al. 2025). That database, telo_database_v2.tsv, is a tab-separated table of 4,051 rows, one per examined species, and a few species appear twice. Each row gives the telomere repeat unit reported for the species, its taxonomy from genus to superkingdom, the assembly the unit was checked on, and how well it is supported:

Support Rows Used by FunFlux strong 2,292 yes weak 698 yes unchecked 629 no none, with no unit 432 no

FunFlux takes the units with strong or weak support, 256 distinct units, as candidate telomere units in every run. Most rows are animals (2,996), while 903 are plants and 126 fungi. The candidates table of each sample says how many species per kingdom carry each unit, as described on Contig summary.

Rule telomere_db downloads the file with curl from links.telomere_db_link, once per output folder, and checks it against parameters.contig_summary.telomere_db_sha256 with sha256sum -c. It keeps the file as 00.resources/telomeres/telo_database_v2.tsv, with a PROVENANCE.txt beside it that records the source URL, the download date, the checksum and the row count. The template address names one commit of the repository tolkit/a-telomeric-repeat-database on GitHub, so the file behind it does not change. A file that does not match the checksum stops the run with [FunFlux] telomere_db: ..., and the download is kept with the suffix .failed. To move to a newer version of the database, change the link and the checksum together:

curl -L --fail -o telo_database_v2.tsv '<the new address>'
sha256sum telo_database_v2.tsv   # put the 64 characters into parameters.contig_summary.telomere_db_sha256

A new checksum re-runs telomere_db, then telomere_units and the contig summary of every sample. There is no local-copy key: the file is 0.6 MB, and a run needs network access to raw.githubusercontent.com once per output folder. The repository publishes no licence file, so FunFlux neither ships the database nor mirrors it. It is downloaded on your machine at run time, as the Tiberius model is. Cite it through the tidk paper and the address, as listed on Citation and references.

docs.title: ChroQueTas and the FungAMR database
docs.text:
The AMR screen, also called the resistance-mutation screen, is off by default. It runs ChroQueTas against the FungAMR database, which lists point mutations with the evidence for or against resistance to antifungal drugs and fungicides, as described on Antifungal resistance mutations. ChroQueTas is one bash script, and its authors keep the database prepared for it in the same GitHub repository, nmquijada/ChroQueTas. Both are licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so FunFlux does not ship or mirror them, and does not change them.

With parameters.amr.chroquetas: on, rule chroquetas_db downloads three files with curl from links.chroquetas_link, once per output folder, into 00.resources/chroquetas/:

File at the link Kept as Checked against bin/ChroQueTas.sh (29,202 bytes) ChroQueTas.sh parameters.amr.chroquetas_script_sha256 FungAMR_db/db-v20250811.tgz (137,391 bytes) unpacked into FungAMR_db/, one folder per species; the archive is then deleted parameters.amr.chroquetas_db_sha256 LICENSE LICENSE its checksum is recorded in PROVENANCE.txt

The rule checks the script and the archive with sha256sum -c before anything runs or is unpacked. It then writes species.txt, which lists the 57 species folders one per line, and PROVENANCE.txt, which records the three addresses, the download date, the checksums, the species count and the licence. The template address names one commit, the one tagged v1.0.1, so the files behind it do not change. A file that does not match its checksum stops the run with [FunFlux] chroquetas_db: ... and is kept with the suffix .failed.

To move to a newer version, read the new script and its licence, then change the link and both checksums together. FunFlux reads the files ChroQueTas 1.0.1 writes, so a version that writes them differently stops amr_chroquetas with an error and needs a newer FunFlux.

BASE=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nmquijada/ChroQueTas/<commit>
curl -L --fail -o ChroQueTas.sh "$BASE/bin/ChroQueTas.sh"
curl -L --fail -o db.tgz "$BASE/FungAMR_db/<archive name>"
sha256sum ChroQueTas.sh db.tgz   # into chroquetas_script_sha256 and chroquetas_db_sha256

The archive name, db-v20250811.tgz, is fixed in FunFlux, so a newer database under another name needs a newer FunFlux. A new link or checksum re-runs chroquetas_db, then amr_chroquetas of every sample. There is no local-copy key: the files are small, and a run with the AMR screen on needs network access to raw.githubusercontent.com once per output folder.

docs.title: PhiX genome
docs.text: Only illumina and hybrid mode use the PhiX genome. links.phix_link points at NCBI's PhiX174 genome (GCF_000819615.1, 2 kB compressed), the control that Illumina libraries are spiked with. download_phix fetches it with curl once per output folder into 00.resources/phix/, and build_phix indexes it there for bowtie2. map_phix then removes the read pairs of every sample that map to it. In these modes an empty value stops the run before any job starts.

docs.title: Medaka model
docs.text:
A Medaka model is needed in longread and hybrid only, for ONT samples, unless medaka_model: false. Medaka 2.2.2 ships the weights of four models. For any other model it downloads them the first time the model is used, so the run needs network access once.

The download happens in check_medaka_model, before the assembler starts and on the computer that runs Snakemake. A named model is checked and its weights fetched. With medaka_model: auto, the model is worked out from the basecaller tag in the read headers, and its weights are fetched. Medaka keeps them in its conda environment, or in ~/.medaka/data when it cannot write there, so polishing needs no network. See The Medaka model.

docs.title: Pointing a key at a local copy
docs.text:
Five database keys name a folder on your own disk. The table gives what each folder holds, what FunFlux checks before any job starts, and what the run does with the folder:

Key The folder holds Checked before any job starts What the run does directories.blast_db the core_nt files, taxdb.btd, taxdb.bti, nodes.dmp, names.dmp NOTE when the folder is missing; with the screen on, the dry run stops without nodes.dmp or names.dmp reads it directories.eggnog_db the files download_eggnog_data.py writes NOTE when the folder is missing reads it directories.funannotate_db the unpacked funannotate database, or nothing yet the parameters.prediction.busco_db set, when a funannotate database is present downloads the database if it is missing; rewrites the paths inside it directories.antismash_db clusterblast/ and the other database folders the run stops when the folder is missing or has no clusterblast/ links its entries into 00.resources/antismash/databases/ directories.unite_db unite_its_sintax.fasta, uncompressed the run stops when the file is missing links the file into 00.resources/unite/

FunFlux turns each of these paths into an absolute one, measured from the launch folder. Write them as absolute paths. Every key is listed on Configuration.

docs.title: Licensed and external tools
docs.text:
Three tools are not installed by conda: InterProScan, which every run needs, and the optional GeneMark-ES and SignalP 6. You obtain them yourself, and FunFlux calls them from its own environments. Install InterProScan before the first run. For each tool, this page explains how to obtain and install it, how FunFlux runs it and what happens without it.

Tool Needed Licence Config keys Without it GeneMark-ES optional free for academic, non-profit and US government users; the key expires one year after download directories.genemark_dir, parameters.genemark.mode funannotate predict runs without GeneMark-ES SignalP 6 optional, off by default DTU: download page for academic users, others contact DTU files.signalp6_archive, parameters.signalp6.* no secretome annotation InterProScan 5.78-109.0 required Apache-2.0 files.iprscan the run stops: InterProScan cannot be switched off

The licences of GeneMark-ES and SignalP 6 limit who may use them freely, and so do two of the databases InterProScan searches in every run: commercial users of PROSITE pay a yearly licence fee, and SMART is free for academic users only. The licence terms in full are on Licensing.

The optional AMR screen, also called the resistance-mutation screen, runs ChroQueTas. ChroQueTas is not installed by conda either, and its licence allows non-commercial use only. You do not download it yourself. With parameters.amr.chroquetas: on, the workflow downloads it at run time, as described in ChroQueTas and the FungAMR database.

Terms used on this page
