docs.title: Building the environments in advance
docs.text:
The environments can be built before the first run, with one command:

snakemake --sdm conda --conda-create-envs-only --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

This builds every environment the configured run needs and exits without starting a job. Snakemake plans the run to find them, so the configuration must pass FunFlux's checks (mode, input folder, annotation table). With --list-conda-envs in place of --conda-create-envs-only, Snakemake prints each environment file with the folder it is built in.

Next, run snakemake download_all to fetch, in the same way, every file the run downloads: databases, models, a named BUSCO lineage and the Medaka weights. It is needed only when Snakemake itself will run without internet, as in a batch job on a compute node. See Preparation, on a computer with internet.

docs.title: Sharing environments: --conda-prefix
docs.text:
Without --conda-prefix, the environments are built in .snakemake/conda/ of the launch folder, so all runs started from one clone share them. --conda-prefix puts them in a folder of your choice, which several clones, users or projects can share:

snakemake --sdm conda --conda-prefix /path/to/funflux_envs --cores 24 \
    --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

export SNAKEMAKE_CONDA_PREFIX=/path/to/funflux_envs before the command has the same effect.

  • Each environment is a folder named <hash>_, a code Snakemake computes from the yaml file, the pin file and the path of the prefix. A FunFlux update that changes a yaml or pin file builds a new folder beside the old one.
  • Moving or renaming the prefix rebuilds every environment, because conda environments contain absolute paths. In an output folder made from the same launch folder, Snakemake then re-runs every finished step that has an environment, and the steps after it, as described under Conda environments. Choose the prefix once.
  • Old folders stay until you delete them. To see which ones are in use, run --list-conda-envs with the same --conda-prefix and configuration. A configuration without the screen or SignalP 6 lists fewer. A <hash>_ folder, with its <hash>_.* files, can be deleted when no configuration or clone using the prefix lists it. In a shared prefix, collect the lists of all configurations first. Do not use --conda-cleanup-envs for this, because in Snakemake 9.14.6 it deletes the environments of the current workflow.
  • With the screen or SignalP 6, the prefix must be writable by whoever runs FunFlux. BlobTools writes its taxonomy index (nodesDB.txt) into its environment, and install_signalp6 installs SignalP 6 into the signalp6 environment.
  • A rebuilt signalp6 environment no longer contains SignalP 6. The next run stops in signalp6_annotation and asks you to delete 00.resources/signalp6/installation.json. See Troubleshooting.
  • With SignalP 6 on, everyone who uses the prefix also uses the SignalP 6 installed in it, which is licensed to the person who installed it.
  • On a cluster, the prefix must be on storage the compute nodes see, under the same path. See Shared storage.

Continue with Reference databases and Licensed and external tools, then Quick start.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This page goes step by step from cloning FunFlux to a finished run, then lists the main results and what a run costs in time, memory and disk space. The example annotates one assembled genome in contigs mode. For reads, step 4 sets another mode and input folder and step 5 needs a real directories.blast_db, while the other steps are the same. If you are not sure which mode fits your data, see Choosing a mode.

Terms used on this page

conda environment a separate software installation for one tool, in which its rules run; with --sdm conda, Snakemake builds each one from workflow/envs/ rule one step of the workflow as Snakemake defines it, such as filter_contigs; the console and the log files in logs/ use its name the screen the contamination and mitochondrion screen: BLAST against core_nt, BlobTools, the mitochondrion screen and the contig selector; in contigs mode only with parameters.contigs.screen: true launch folder the folder Snakemake is started from, normally the FunFlux repository; relative paths are read from it, and .snakemake/ is created there funannotate database the frozen snapshot of funannotate's data, such as Swiss-Prot, Pfam, the BUSCO set and stored AUGUSTUS models, downloaded once from Zenodo into directories.funannotate_db dry run a Snakemake run with -n: FunFlux checks the configuration and the inputs, and Snakemake lists the jobs it plans without running any; it takes seconds job one run of a rule, for one sample or once for the whole run; the dry run lists the jobs it plans AMR screen the optional resistance-mutation screen, off by default (parameters.amr.chroquetas): ChroQueTas looks in each genome for the changes FungAMR lists for the species; results in 05.amr/

docs.title: 1. Clone FunFlux and install Snakemake
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install Snakemake in an environment of its own:

git clone https://github.com/iLivius/FunFlux.git
cd FunFlux
conda create -c conda-forge -c bioconda -n snakemake "snakemake>=9.14.6,<10"
conda activate snakemake

conda must be 24.7.1 or newer (conda --version), because Snakemake 9.14.6 stops with an error on an older one. On a cluster whose conda module is older, install Miniforge in your own folder and use its conda. Set conda config --set channel_priority strict once, or Snakemake prints a warning.

FunFlux v2 was developed and tested with Snakemake 9.14.6, and it stops at start-up on an older version. Later 9.x releases should work, while 10 or later has not been tested. The analysis tools are not installed in this environment: with --sdm conda, Snakemake builds the conda environment of each tool from its pinned package list in workflow/envs/ the first time a rule needs it.

Run every command below from the repository folder, where Snakemake finds workflow/Snakefile without being told. See Installation for the details.

docs.title: 2. Provide what FunFlux does not download
docs.text:
Apart from the resources below, FunFlux downloads what it needs itself (step 8). Download or install these yourself before the first run that needs them, and give their paths in step 5.

Config key What Size Needed directories.eggnog_db eggNOG-mapper data of eggNOG 5.0.2 (eggnog.db, eggnog_proteins.dmnd) 48 GB always files.iprscan interproscan.sh of a local InterProScan 5.78-109.0 (not on bioconda) about 50 GB installed always directories.blast_db NCBI core_nt, with taxdb.btd, taxdb.bti, nodes.dmp and names.dmp in the same folder 264 GB (build of 11 July 2026) illumina, longread, hybrid; contigs with the screen directories.genemark_dir GeneMark-ES, with its licence key in ~/.gm_key optional files.signalp6_archive the SignalP 6 archive from DTU optional

core_nt is needed only when the contamination and mitochondrion screen runs. The two optional tools, GeneMark-ES and SignalP 6, are licensed. How to get each resource is explained on Reference databases and Licensed and external tools.

docs.title: 3. Copy the configuration template
docs.text:
Make your own copy of the configuration template, for steps 4 and 5 to fill in:

cp config/config.yaml config/config_custom.yaml

Edit the copy. config/config_custom.yaml is listed in .gitignore, so it stays out of commits and git pull leaves it alone.

docs.title: 4. Set the mode and the input folder
docs.text:
mode selects the input mode, and the input key of that mode names the folder of the input files (hybrid has two such keys). The example reads assemblies:

mode: contigs

input:
  contigs_dir: /path/to/assemblies      # SAMPLE1.fasta -> sample SAMPLE1

The four modes take their input from these keys and file names:

mode Input key File names illumina input.illumina_dir {sample}_R1.<ext> and {sample}_R2.<ext> longread input.longread_dir {sample}_ont.<ext> or {sample}_pacbio.<ext> (PacBio HiFi) hybrid input.illumina_dir and input.longread_dir (may be the same folder) both of the above contigs input.contigs_dir {sample}.fasta, {sample}.fa or {sample}.fna, uncompressed

<ext> is fastq, fq, fastq.gz or fq.gz, the same for all files of one kind in a batch. The file name without its suffix is the sample name. It appears in every output path and becomes the locus-tag prefix of every predicted gene. In contigs mode every file in the folder whose name contains a dot is read as a sample, so keep only the FASTA files there. The naming rules and mixed batches are described on Choosing a mode.

docs.title: 5. Set the output folder and the database paths
docs.text:
These keys tell FunFlux where to write the results, and where to find the databases, InterProScan and the annotation parameter table of step 6:

directories:
  output_dir:     /path/to/results/run1
  eggnog_db:      /path/to/eggnog_db
  funannotate_db: /path/to/funannotate_db
  blast_db:       /path/to/blast_db      # illumina, longread, hybrid; contigs only with the screen

files:
  annotation_params: /path/to/annotation_parameters.tsv
  iprscan:           /path/to/interproscan-5.78-109.0/interproscan.sh

resources:
  threads: 24
  • funannotate_db may name a folder that does not exist yet, and the first run downloads the database into it (step 8).
  • A relative path is read from the launch folder, the folder you start Snakemake in, not from the folder of the config file.
  • resources.threads is the thread ceiling of the rules, and --cores should get the same number.
  • The download links under links: and everything under parameters: can stay as they are.

Let one run repair the paths in funannotate_db before another run uses that folder

FunFlux repairs the absolute paths stored inside the funannotate_db folder without a lock. Let one run get past this repair, rule normalize_funannotate_db, before you start another one on the same folder, as Reference databases explains.

The optional keys switch on the two licensed tools, point FunFlux at databases you already have, or add the screen in contigs mode.

To Set let funannotate use GeneMark-ES directories.genemark_dir: /path/to/gmes_linux_64_4 (absolute path; licence key in ~/.gm_key) predict signal peptides with SignalP 6 files.signalp6_archive: /path/to/signalp-6.0i.fast.tar.gz (absolute path) and parameters.signalp6.mode: fast use an antiSMASH database you already have directories.antismash_db: /path/to/antismash_db (the folder that holds clusterblast/) use a UNITE file you already have directories.unite_db: /path/to/unite (the folder that holds an uncompressed unite_its_sintax.fasta) find the mitochondrial genome and get a BLAST taxonomy per contig parameters.contigs.screen: true and directories.blast_db

Every key is listed on Configuration.

docs.title: 6. Write the annotation parameter table
docs.text:
For each sample, the annotation parameter table gives the species, a protein FASTA of related fungi and, optionally, a stored AUGUSTUS model. It has one line per sample, with three or four columns separated by tabs, and lines starting with # are skipped. This command writes the table of the example:

printf 'SAMPLE1\tFusarium graminearum\t/path/to/fusarium_proteins.faa\t-\n' \
    > /path/to/annotation_parameters.tsv
Column Content In the example 1 the sample name from step 4 SAMPLE1 2 the species, genus and species; the result files are named after it Fusarium graminearum, giving Fusarium_graminearum_SAMPLE1.gbk 3 a protein FASTA of closely related fungi /path/to/fusarium_proteins.faa 4, optional a stored AUGUSTUS model: - or no fourth column, the default, makes funannotate train AUGUSTUS on the genome's own conserved (BUSCO) genes; a name, one of the folder names in /path/to/funannotate_db/trained_species/ such as fusarium_graminearum, makes AUGUSTUS use that stored model as it is instead -

Column 3 takes the predicted proteins of a species close to yours, for example the RefSeq proteome of a species of the same genus. As evidence for its gene models, funannotate aligns them to the genome, together with UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot, which it always adds. The file must exist and must not be empty. To download a proteome from NCBI, put the accession of its genome in place of <accession>, for example GCF_000143535.2 for Botrytis cinerea B05.10:

curl -L -o proteins.zip \
  "https://api.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/v2/genome/accession/<accession>/download?include_annotation_type=PROT_FASTA"
unzip proteins.zip      # gives ncbi_dataset/data/<accession>/protein.faa

Whether to let AUGUSTUS train or to name a stored AUGUSTUS model is discussed on Gene prediction. What each column does, and what the dry run checks, is described under Annotation parameter table.

docs.title: 7. Dry run
docs.text:
Before the real run, check the configuration and the plan with a dry run:

snakemake --sdm conda --cores 24 --configfile config/config_custom.yaml -n

-n builds the plan and stops. FunFlux checks the configuration and the input files before it plans any job, so the dry run takes seconds and writes nothing to output_dir. It stops at the first problem with a [FunFlux] line that names the key, file or sample to fix. For the example it prints, after the banner:

Mode: contigs — Annotation of fungal genome assemblies you already have.
[FunFlux] NOTE: contigs mode without parameters.contigs.screen: your FASTA gets no contamination or mitochondrion screen. If its headers are SPAdes-style (>NODE_<n>_length_<L>_cov_<C>), rule filter_contigs drops contigs under 500 bp or under 2x coverage; otherwise it only cuts each header at its first space or tab. A mitochondrial genome in your FASTA, if present, will be annotated as nuclear. Set parameters.contigs.screen: true to find and split it off (needs directories.blast_db).
Decontamination mode: off (discard_no_hit=false).
GeneMark-ES: off (funannotate runs its no-GeneMark branch).
Tiberius: on (its gene models join the others in EVidenceModeler, weight 1).
SignalP 6: off.
Contig summary: telomere motif auto (the repeat unit is chosen from the data), a telomere from 5 tandem copies within 25000 bp of a contig end, an rDNA array from 3 rDNA unit(s).
AMR screen: off.
Sample SAMPLE1 will be processed.
AUGUSTUS: SAMPLE1 is trained on its BUSCO genes (checked once the database is unpacked).

The Decontamination mode line is printed in every run, and without the screen it has no effect.

Snakemake then prints Conda environment ... will be created. for every environment not built yet (14 here), followed by the jobs it plans:

Job stats:
job                           count
--------------------------  -------
all                               1
antismash_annotation              1
antismash_db                      1
augustus_model_check              1
cleanup                           1
completeness                      1
contig_summary                    1
eggnog_annotation                 1
filter_contigs                    1
funannotate_annotation            1
funannotate_db                    1
funannotate_prediction            1
funannotate_preprocess            1
genome_assembly_evaluation        1
iprscan_annotation                1
its_classification                1
its_extraction                    1
its_windows                       1
multiqc                           1
normalize_funannotate_db          1
repeat_masking                    1
telomere_db                       1
telomere_units                    1
tiberius_gff3                     1
tiberius_model                    1
tiberius_prediction               1
unite_db                          1
unite_identified                  1
total                            28

One block per job follows, each with the reason it runs. Each further sample adds 19 jobs, and other settings change the plan as follows:

Setting Jobs funannotate database already in funannotate_db no funannotate_db directories.antismash_db or directories.unite_db set antismash_db_local or unite_db_local instead of the download job GeneMark-ES on genemark_check per sample: GeneMark-ES on a 200 kb slice of the masked genome before gene prediction (about a minute), so that an expired licence key stops the run before funannotate predict starts instead of partway through it SignalP 6 on install_signalp6 once, signalp6_annotation per sample parameters.tiberius.mode: off no tiberius_model, and no tiberius_prediction and tiberius_gff3 per sample parameters.its.unite_identified_only: false no unite_identified: SINTAX classifies against the whole UNITE release parameters.contigs.screen: true 8 per sample: map_contigs, blast_contigs, blob_json, blob_table, select_contigs, screen_mitochondria, finalize_assembly, separate_mitochondria parameters.amr.chroquetas: on chroquetas_db once, amr_chroquetas per sample: the AMR screen for antifungal resistance mutations (Antifungal resistance mutations)

With the funannotate database present, a local antiSMASH database, and GeneMark-ES and SignalP 6 on, the plan has 30 jobs. The read-based modes plan more jobs per sample, for the read processing, the assembly, the polishing and the mapping QC:

Mode Jobs in the first run of one sample contigs, the example 28 illumina 43 longread 41 (PacBio HiFi) or 43 (ONT with Medaka) hybrid 58 (PacBio HiFi) or 60 (ONT with Medaka)

How these counts are made up is explained on Running FunFlux.

A dry run that passes does not show that the eggNOG data, InterProScan and core_nt are usable

The dry run checks these paths only in part.

Path What the dry run checks What happens directories.eggnog_db, files.iprscan existence only a missing eggnog_db folder or iprscan file prints a NOTE (... does not exist on this machine; the eggNOG step will fail without it.) and the dry run goes on; wrong content there goes unnoticed until eggNOG-mapper or InterProScan fails, after gene prediction, hours into the run directories.antismash_db, directories.unite_db clusterblast/ and unite_its_sintax.fasta the dry run stops without them directories.blast_db, with the screen on nodes.dmp and names.dmp a folder without either stops the dry run with MissingInputException in rule blob_json; a folder without core_nt passes the dry run and fails when blast_contigs starts

docs.title: 8. Run
docs.text:
When the dry run shows the plan you expect, start the run with the same command without -n:

snakemake --sdm conda --cores 24 --configfile config/config_custom.yaml

--cores is the only CPU setting of this command: give it the value of resources.threads, and do not add --jobs or -j. Each CPU-bound rule declares its threads, and Snakemake runs jobs side by side while their threads fit into --cores. The caps of all rules are listed on CPU cores and threads.

On a cluster, either let Snakemake send each step to the scheduler (--executor slurm --jobs N), or run this command inside one batch job on one node. Both ways, and the preparation for compute nodes without internet, are described on On a cluster.

Snakemake keeps its records and the conda environments in .snakemake/ inside the launch folder. Launch from the same folder every time, or add --conda-prefix /path/to/conda_envs, so that the environments are built once.

After an interruption, run the same command: finished jobs are kept and the rest is redone. Snakemake asks for --unlock after a killed run, and for --rerun-incomplete when a job left incomplete output.

The first run downloads and builds what the table lists. The environments and the funannotate database are built once and reused by every run that points at the same folder. The files under 00.resources/ are fetched once per output folder, while with the automatic lineage the BUSCO data are fetched again in every BUSCO job.

What Where Size When conda environments (14 in the example) .snakemake/conda/, or the --conda-prefix folder about 20 GB, plus conda's package cache first use of each funannotate database snapshot (Zenodo record 23265189) and its .sha256 file directories.funannotate_db 2.1 GB archive; 6.1 GB unpacked, 8.1 GB with the archive when funannotate-db-info.txt is missing there antiSMASH 8.0.4 databases 00.resources/antismash/databases/ about 9.4 GB unless directories.antismash_db is set UNITE SINTAX reference, release 19.02.2025, all eukaryotes 00.resources/unite/unite_its_sintax.fasta 35.7 MB download, 207 MB unpacked unless directories.unite_db is set Tiberius fungi model 00.resources/tiberius/model/ 30 MB download, 31 MB unpacked while parameters.tiberius.mode is on, the default telomere repeat database of tidk 00.resources/telomeres/telo_database_v2.tsv 0.6 MB always BUSCO lineage datasets 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/busco/busco_tmp/, deleted after the job eukaryota_odb12 29 MB, compressed, plus 8 MB of placement files for the automatic lineage step and the lineage dataset BUSCO places the genome in every BUSCO job, for every sample, with parameters.busco.lineage: auto; a named lineage is fetched once per output folder into 00.resources/busco/

Three of these downloads are checked with sha256sum -c before they are used:

Download Checked against funannotate archive its .sha256 file; a mismatch stops the run with the instruction to delete both files and start again Tiberius model parameters.tiberius.model_sha256 telomere repeat database parameters.contig_summary.telomere_db_sha256

For the UNITE file, 00.resources/unite/PROVENANCE.txt records the URL, download date, md5 and size. For the telomere repeat database, 00.resources/telomeres/PROVENANCE.txt records the URL, download date, checksum and row count.

InterProScan also asks EBI's lookup service for matches already computed, which only saves time (see Functional annotation). The read-based modes also download the PhiX genome (illumina, hybrid) and the Medaka model for ONT samples.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The table lists the main result files. Paths are relative to output_dir, {sample} is the sample name, and <Genus_species> is the species column of the annotation table with an underscore for the space.

What File Genome that QUAST, BUSCO, the ITS steps and funannotate read 02.assembly/{sample}/contigs_final.fasta Assembly statistics (QUAST) 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/quast/report.tsv Completeness (BUSCO) 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/busco/short_summary.specific.<lineage>.{sample}.txt ITS1, ITS2 and full ITS, one record per rDNA unit 03.taxonomy/{sample}/{sample}.ITS1.fasta, {sample}.ITS2.fasta, {sample}.full.fasta ITS copies found, and records rejected by the length check 03.taxonomy/{sample}/{sample}_ITS_copies.txt ITS classification against UNITE 03.taxonomy/{sample}/{sample}_ITS1_taxonomy.txt, {sample}_ITS2_taxonomy.txt Genome as annotated, contigs sorted by length and renamed scaffold_1, scaffold_2, ... 04.annotation/{sample}/contigs_sort.fasta Contigs removed by funannotate clean before annotation 04.annotation/{sample}/contigs_removed_by_clean.txt Gene models and functional annotation 04.annotation/{sample}/funannotate/annotate_results/<Genus_species>_{sample}.gbk, .gff3, .tbl, .sqn, .proteins.fa, .annotations.txt InterProScan, eggNOG-mapper, antiSMASH 04.annotation/{sample}/iprscan/interproscan_out.xml, eggnog/{sample}.emapper.annotations, antismash/index.html SignalP 6 04.annotation/{sample}/signalp6/prediction_results.txt Antifungal resistance mutations, with the AMR screen on 05.amr/{sample}/amr_summary.tsv QUAST and BUSCO of all samples on one page 06.report/multiqc_report.html Logs, one per rule and sample logs/

QUAST, BUSCO and the ITS files use the contig names of contigs_final.fasta, while the annotation uses the scaffold_N names. The annotated_as column of 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/contig_summary.tsv links the two. Every file is described on Output files.

docs.title: Run time and disk
docs.text:
As the table below shows, plan for several hours per genome and for about 16 GB of memory for Tiberius.

What Time, memory or space One fungal genome in contigs mode several hours InterProScan usually a few hours for a fungal proteome Tiberius about half an hour for a 40 Mb genome, with about 16 GB of memory Output folder of one sample in the order of 10 GB A downloaded antiSMASH database about 9.4 GB more in 00.resources/ funannotate database, outside the output folder 8.1 GB conda environments, outside the output folder about 20 GB for the 14 of the example, 22 GB with SignalP 6

How long the steps take is described on Run time, and where the space goes on Disk use.

docs.title: BLAST hit depth
docs.text:
This page explains how many BLAST hits FunFlux keeps for each contig, and why. Read it before you change parameters.blast_max_target_seqs or parameters.blast_max_hsps, or when you compare genus calls with those of FunFlux 1.1.x.

Terms used on this page

the screen the contamination and mitochondrion screen of the draft: BLAST, BlobTools, the mitochondrion screen and the contig selector; in contigs mode only with parameters.contigs.screen: true core_nt the NCBI core nucleotide BLAST database, which the screen searches every draft contig against; you download it, with its taxonomy files, into directories.blast_db subject the BLAST word for a database sequence a contig matched, the contig being the query; BLAST keeps up to 50 per contig (blast_max_target_seqs) HSP high-scoring segment pair, one local alignment between a contig and a subject; BLAST keeps up to blast_max_hsps (5) per subject FunFluxL, FunFluxL+ two of the v1 workflows that FunFlux v2 replaces: FunFluxL for long reads and the unpublished FunFluxL+ for hybrid data clean circle a contig the assembler recorded as circular, not as a repeat and not as an alternative copy of another contig genus filter the setting parameters.decontamination.mode: include or exclude, under which the contig selector keeps or removes contigs by the genus BlobTools gave them

The contamination and mitochondrion screen runs one BLAST search per draft assembly. Rule blast_contigs runs it with megablast against core_nt and an e-value of 1e-5, and in hybrid rule blast_guide_contigs does the same for the guide assembly, with the same two keys. Two programs read its result table, BlobTools and the mitochondrion screen:

---
config:
  themeVariables:
    fontSize: 14px
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 35
    rankSpacing: 35
---
flowchart TD
    C([draft contigs]) --> B[megablast against core_nt<br/>blast_contigs]
    B --> T([BLAST table<br/>by default at most 50 subjects<br/>per contig, 5 HSPs per subject])
    T --> BT[BlobTools<br/>assigns each contig a genus]
    T --> MS[mitochondrion screen<br/>looks for mitochondrial contigs]

Two BLAST options decide how much of the search is kept. FunFlux v2 sets them to 50 and 5 in every mode.

Key Default blastn option blastn help text (BLAST+ 2.16.0) parameters.blast_max_target_seqs 50 -max_target_seqs "Maximum number of aligned sequences to keep (value of 5 or more is recommended)" parameters.blast_max_hsps 5 -max_hsps "Set maximum number of HSPs per subject sequence to save for each query" Workflow or source max_target_seqs / max_hsps e-value FunFlux 1.1.x (Illumina) 10 / 1 1e-5 FunFluxL and FunFluxL+ 50 / 5 1e-5 FunFlux v2, every mode 50 / 5 1e-5 BlobTools manual, for its "most accurate results" 10 / 1 1e-25 BlobToolKit tutorial "Adding hits" 10 / 1 1e-25 Sanger Tree of Life BlobToolKit pipeline 10 / 1 1e-10

FunFlux v2 keeps the values of FunFluxL. They do not come from a published comparison, and the three BlobTools sources do not explain theirs either. The sources' 10 / 1 serves the taxonomy alone. FunFlux v2 also reads the table in its mitochondrion screen, which needs more than one HSP per subject (below). The e-value of 1e-5 is more permissive than the sources' 1e-10 or 1e-25. The difference matters only for weak, short matches, which can give a contig a genus where a stricter cut-off would leave it without a hit. A contig that matches a database sequence over hundreds of bases has an e-value far below all three cut-offs.

FunFlux 1.1.x used 10 / 1, so its genus calls can differ from those of v2, as described in What changes with fewer hits.

docs.title: Five HSPs: what the mitochondrion screen needs
docs.text:
The mitochondrion screen, rule screen_mitochondria, reads the BLAST column qcovs ("Query Coverage Per Subject"). qcovs is the share of the contig covered by all the HSPs that BLAST saved for one subject. With -max_hsps 1 only the best HSP is saved, and qcovs equals qcovhsp ("Query Coverage Per HSP"). Rearrangements, indels or a different start position on the circle can make a mitochondrial genome align to its closest reference in several blocks. With one HSP per subject, such a genome then looks partly covered.

For each contig, the mitochondrion screen takes the highest qcovs among its hits to organelle genomes and confirms the contig as follows:

Mode Evidence from the assembler A contig is confirmed when its highest qcovs contigs, illumina, the hybrid guide none reaches mitochondria.min_direct_blast_qcov (default 35). A contig with a weaker organelle hit becomes a mitochondrial_candidate, which stays in contigs_final.fasta and goes through the nuclear gene prediction longread, the hybrid long-read assembly the depth, or a clean circle reaches mitochondria.very_strong_qcov (70) on its own, or reaches min_direct_blast_qcov but then only together with the assembler's depth or a clean circle

One HSP per subject can leave a complete mitochondrial genome unconfirmed

With one HSP per subject, only the best block of a multi-block match counts. A complete mitochondrial genome that aligns to its nearest core_nt reference in many pieces can then fall below min_direct_blast_qcov. The mitochondrion screen is described on Mitochondria.

The default of 5 HSPs has not been compared with other values on a public genome.

docs.title: Fifty target sequences: BLAST's own advice
docs.text:
BLAST applies -max_target_seqs during the search, not as a filter on the finished, ranked list of hits. A small value can therefore drop subjects that would have ranked higher (Shah et al. 2019). NCBI's reply confirmed the mechanism, fixed a related bug in BLAST+ 2.8.1 and made BLAST+ warn when fewer than five subjects are requested (Madden et al. 2019). BLAST+ 2.16.0 prints:

Warning: [blastn] Examining 5 or more matches is recommended

FunFlux uses 50, the value of FunFluxL; the BlobTools sources in the table above use 10. Both meet NCBI's advice of at least five.

docs.title: What changes with fewer hits
docs.text:
FunFlux 1.1.x took 10 / 1 from the BlobToolKit tutorial "Adding hits", which prepares a BLAST table for the taxonomy only, with -max_target_seqs 10 -max_hsps 1 -evalue 1e-25. FunFlux v2 also reads the table for its mitochondrion screen, which needs the coverage that one HSP per subject cannot measure. Keeping fewer subjects and HSPs has these effects:

  • Genus calls. BlobTools' bestsum rule sums the bit scores of all saved hits per taxon. The number of subjects and HSPs kept can therefore change the genus a contig is assigned to. This matters most for a fungus whose own genus has few reference sequences in core_nt. Its contigs are then called from related genera, and the call can differ between settings.
  • Mitochondrion screen. The coverage of a multi-block match is that of its best block only, as explained above.
  • Size of the BLAST table. At 50/5 the table holds several times more lines than at 10/1, but it stays a small text file.
  • Run time. It does not change in practice, because BLAST computes the alignments either way.

The genus calls matter only with a genus filter, decontamination.mode include or exclude. With off, the default, every contig is kept whatever its genus, so the genus calls change no delivered genome file. See Decontamination.

docs.title: Notices and re-runs
docs.text:
Both values must be whole numbers of at least 1. With the screen on, two notices can print when the workflow starts:

[FunFlux] NOTE: parameters.blast_max_hsps is 1. Below 5, BLAST reports the coverage of a multi-block mitochondrial match as that of its best block only, which weakens the mitochondrion screen (a complete mitogenome can fall under min_direct_blast_qcov).
[FunFlux] NOTE: parameters.blast_max_target_seqs is 3; BLAST recommends 5 or more.

The first notice, on blast_max_hsps, prints when that value is below 5 and mitochondria.mode is not off. The second, on blast_max_target_seqs, prints when that value is below 5.

Changing either value runs the BLAST search again.

docs.title: Reproducing FunFlux 1.1.x
docs.text:
Set these values only to reproduce results of FunFlux 1.1.x:

parameters:
  blast_max_target_seqs: 10
  blast_max_hsps: 1

The run then prints the blast_max_hsps notice, because the mitochondrion screen is weaker with one HSP. The 10 / 1 setting has not been run with v2 yet.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Shah N., Nute M.G., Warnow T., Pop M. (2019). Misunderstood parameter of NCBI BLAST impacts the correctness of bioinformatics workflows. Bioinformatics 35(9):1613-1614. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bty833
  • Madden T.L., Busby B., Ye J. (2019). Reply to the paper: Misunderstood parameters of NCBI BLAST impacts the correctness of bioinformatics workflows. Bioinformatics 35(15):2699-2700. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bty1026
  • BlobToolKit, "Adding hits": https://blobtoolkit.genomehubs.org/blobtools2/blobtools2-tutorials/adding-data-to-a-dataset/adding-hits/
  • BlobTools manual, "Taxonomy file": https://blobtools.readme.io/docs/taxonomy-file
  • Sanger Tree of Life, BlobToolKit pipeline, BLAST settings in conf/modules.config: https://github.com/sanger-tol/blobtoolkit

docs.title: Filtlong guidance in hybrid mode
docs.text:
In hybrid mode the Illumina reads of a sample can guide Filtlong, the filter that chooses which ONT reads go into the assembly. The guidance is off by default, and the ONT reads then get the same length and quality filter as in longread mode. This page gives the reasons for that default, describes what the guidance does when it is on, and shows how to compare the settings on your own data.

With short_read_guidance: true, Filtlong scores each ONT read by how much of it the Illumina reads confirm. It trims unconfirmed bases from the read ends and removes every stretch of 1,000 or more consecutive unconfirmed bases, splitting the read there. PacBio HiFi reads are never guided.

---
config:
  themeVariables:
    fontSize: 14px
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 35
    rankSpacing: 35
---
flowchart TD
    IL([Illumina pairs]) --> G[SPAdes guide assembly<br/>and its screen]
    G --> SEL([selected pairs<br/>properly paired<br/>on the screened guide])
    ONT([raw ONT reads]) --> F[Filtlong]
    SEL -.->|"only with<br/>short_read_guidance: true"| F
    F --> OUT([filtered ONT reads<br/>to hifiasm or Flye])

Terms used on this page

Filtlong guidance the hybrid setting short_read_guidance: true, off by default: Filtlong scores each ONT read by k-mer matches to the selected pairs and can cut unmatched stretches plain filter the Filtlong run with only the length and quality settings of longread mode: --min_length, --keep_percent, --length_weight and, if set, --target_bases guide assembly the SPAdes assembly of the Illumina reads; it is screened, and only the pairs that map to it go on selected pairs the Illumina pairs properly paired on the screened guide assembly, kept in 01.reads/{sample}/selected/; Polypolish corrects with them, and Filtlong uses them when guided properly paired both reads of a pair map to the same contig, in the expected orientation and distance external reference the Filtlong term for reads it judges long reads against instead of their Phred scores; in FunFlux, the selected pairs, only with the guidance on k-mer a short sequence of fixed length; Filtlong compares long reads with the Illumina reads through their 16-mers, k-mers of 16 bases

docs.title: Why it is off by default
docs.text:
Three sources weigh against making the guidance the default:

  • Filtlong's own advice. The Filtlong README says: "I recommend against using short reads as an external reference unless you are very confident in the quality of your short-read set."
  • Measured on bacteria. In BacFlux's tests on five bacterial genomes, guidance turned a 6-contig Shigella flexneri assembly into 40 contigs and cost Enterobacter hormaechei a whole replicon. It helped on one genome of five, the least repetitive one with the deepest Illumina reads.
  • Measured on a fungal genome. On Botrytis cinerea B05.10, with the same 136x ONT reads, the guided hybrid run and the unguided longread run gave almost the same assembly. The guided run has 33 contigs and the unguided run 32, and in both, each of the 18 chromosomes is in one contig (Assembly per mode). The mitochondrion differed: the guided run gave it as one contig of about two copies (175,274 bp), while a later hybrid run with the guidance off gave one circular contig of 82,375 bp, close to the published 82,212 bp (Other results).

Guidance can break an assembly apart at repeats

The Illumina reads cover repeats worst, and the long reads that span repeats are the ones that hold an assembly together. Scoring them low, or cutting them there, can break the assembly apart. On one fungal genome the guidance gained nothing measurable. Switch it on only with deep, even Illumina coverage, and compare the result with an unguided run as described under Comparing the three settings.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Two keys in parameters.hybrid control the guidance, and the filtlong block beside them sets the length and quality filter that every sample gets:

Key Default Effect parameters.hybrid.short_read_guidance false false: the plain length and quality filter of longread mode. true: ONT samples get the selected pairs as Filtlong's reference (-1, -2) parameters.hybrid.filtlong_split 1000 used only with short_read_guidance: true. A whole number of bases, at least 1, adds --trim --split <N>. null scores the reads against the Illumina reads but neither trims nor splits them, because FunFlux adds --trim only together with --split. With the guidance off, a number other than 1000 makes the workflow print parameters.hybrid.filtlong_split is ignored because short_read_guidance is false. parameters.hybrid.filtlong min_length: 1000, keep_percent: 90, length_weight: 10, no target_bases the same filter as in longread mode, for every sample

With the guidance on, Filtlong first scores an ONT read by how much of it the Illumina reads confirm, then trims and splits it at its unconfirmed stretches. What remains is filtered with the same filtlong settings. Rule filter_long_reads runs this command for a guided ONT sample:

filtlong -1 01.reads/{sample}/selected/{sample}_selected_R1.fastq \
    -2 01.reads/{sample}/selected/{sample}_selected_R2.fastq \
    --trim --split 1000 --min_length 1000 --keep_percent 90 --length_weight 10 \
    /path/to/longread_dir/{sample}_ont.fastq.gz > 01.reads/{sample}/long/{sample}_filtered.fastq

When the workflow starts, it prints the decision for every sample. With the guidance on, for example:

[FunFlux] SAMPLE1: ont reads -> Filtlong guided by the Illumina reads, hifiasm --ont, minimap2 map-ont, Medaka.
[FunFlux] SAMPLE2: pacbio reads -> Filtlong not guided, hifiasm, minimap2 map-hifi, no Medaka.

docs.title: The Illumina reads that guide
docs.text:
The pairs that guide Filtlong are the selected pairs, chosen in three steps:

  1. SPAdes assembles the Illumina reads into a guide assembly, which goes through the contamination and mitochondrion screen. With decontamination.mode: off, the default, every guide contig is selected.
  2. The trimmed read pairs are mapped back to the selected guide contigs with bowtie2 (--no-unal).
  3. samtools fastq -f 0x2 writes only the properly paired reads, to 01.reads/{sample}/selected/{sample}_selected_R1.fastq and _R2.fastq. These files are kept after the run.

Polypolish uses these pairs in every run. With the guidance on, Filtlong uses them as its reference too for ONT samples, so it waits for them and starts only after the guide assembly and its screen. With the guidance off, Filtlong and the long-read assembly start at once.

docs.title: What Filtlong does with them
docs.text:
The Filtlong README describes how the scoring, the trimming and the splitting work:

  • With an external reference, Filtlong ignores the Phred scores. It collects the 16-mers of the reference. From short reads, a 16-mer is collected only after it has been seen a few times, so read errors are left out. Each base of a long read then gets a quality of 100 if it lies in such a 16-mer, otherwise 0. The mean quality and the window quality of a read are computed from these values.
  • --trim removes the unmatched bases at the start and end of each read.
  • --split N removes every run of N or more consecutive unmatched bases, and the pieces become separate reads. They replace the original reads before --keep_percent and --target_bases choose the best bases. In the README's words, "A lower value will split more aggressively and a higher value will be more conservative."

With the guidance on, the settings --min_length 1000 --keep_percent 90 --length_weight 10 --trim --split 1000 are the README's "Length priority" example without its --target_bases 500mb. Of --split 1kb the README says: "This larger split value makes Filtlong less likely to split a read [...] This helps to keep the output reads longer."

docs.title: Why PacBio HiFi reads are not guided
docs.text: HiFi (CCS) reads are already accurate, at Q20 and above, and guided filtering would cut them wherever the Illumina coverage has a gap. In hybrid mode, ONT reads are guided only with short_read_guidance: true, while PacBio HiFi reads are never guided. A PacBio HiFi sample gets the plain filter, no Medaka, and Polypolish with its selected pairs.

docs.title: Before you switch it on
docs.text:
Filtlong's FAQ names two cases in which short reads mislead it:

  • Short reads that miss part of the genome. In the FAQ's words, "long reads which span the poor-short-read-coverage part of the genome may be erroneously considered low-quality".
  • Read sets that differ biologically. The FAQ's example is a plasmid present only in the long reads. Filtlong can then remove the long reads of that region.

When either applies, leave the guidance off.

docs.title: Comparing the three settings
docs.text:
The guidance can run with or without splitting, so there are three settings to compare, the default and its two alternatives:

Run Setting What Filtlong does with the ONT reads the default short_read_guidance: false the plain length and quality filter of longread mode guidance short_read_guidance: true, filtlong_split: 1000 scores them against the Illumina reads, trims and splits them guidance without split short_read_guidance: true, filtlong_split: null scores them against the Illumina reads, without trimming or splitting

To compare them on your own data, record for each run the contig count, N50, the mitochondrion's length and topology, and BUSCO. QUAST and BUSCO, in 02.assembly/{sample}/eval/, give the contig count, N50 and completeness. mitochondria/mitochondrial_screen.tsv gives the length of the mitochondrial contig, its topology in the assembler_circular column, and its concatemer_flag, which marks a contig that may hold two copies of the mitochondrial genome joined end to end. The flag is Y only when length_ratio is above 1.5 and the assembler did not record the contig as circular (Mitochondria).

docs.title: ITS on long-read contigs
docs.text:
This page explains why ITSx gets short windows instead of whole contigs, which can make it fail on long-read assemblies. The ITS steps themselves, their settings and their output files are described on ITS taxonomy.

FunFlux v2 cuts the ITS region out of the genome in two steps. First, nhmmer finds every 5.8S gene. ITSx then runs on a short ITS window around each one, turned so that it reads from SSU to LSU. Both steps run in every mode, on contigs_final.fasta.

Terms used on this page

SSU, 5.8S and LSU the small-subunit, 5.8S and large-subunit rRNA genes of one rDNA unit, which reads SSU-ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-LSU rDNA unit one copy of the repeat SSU-ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-LSU; FunFlux counts one per 5.8S gene found, that is, one per ITS window rDNA array the tandem copies of the rDNA unit ITS window the stretch cut around one 5.8S gene, 2,000 bp on each side by default (its.window_flank), turned to read from SSU to LSU before ITSx runs anchor one of the four stretches ITSx finds, at the SSU end, both 5.8S ends and the LSU start; ITS1 and ITS2 are cut between them SINTAX the VSEARCH classifier (vsearch --sintax) that names each ITS1 and ITS2 rank by rank against UNITE, with a confidence for each rank v1 workflows the four workflows FunFlux 2.0.0 replaces: FunFlux 1.x (Illumina), Funnotator (assemblies), FunFluxL (long reads) and the unpublished FunFluxL+ (hybrid)

The table compares the v1 workflows with FunFlux v2.

v1 workflows FunFlux v2 What ITSx gets whole contigs, which can fail on long-read assemblies one window of 4,001 bp (with the default flank) around each 5.8S gene, turned to read from SSU to LSU Run time of ITSx minutes on a whole genome seconds, after a search for the 5.8S genes that takes about a minute for a 40-Mb genome Names of the classified records named after their contig {sample}_ITS1_1, {sample}_ITS2_1 and so on

Because the windows are short and all read in the same direction, ITSx avoids the two failures described below.

docs.title: Cause
docs.text:
On whole long-read contigs, ITSx can fail in two ways, and it then writes either nothing or a wrong ITS2. ITSx finds four 45-bp anchors with nhmmer, at the end of the SSU, at both ends of the 5.8S and at the start of the LSU. It cuts ITS1 and ITS2 between them.

  • A failed strand decision. On a multi-megabase contig ITSx also has to decide which strand to read, and that decision fails when the rDNA array lies on the minus strand. ITSx then reports Domains found in wrong order, sequence may be chimeric, with SSU seems to overlap 5.8S and LSU seems to overlap 5.8S, and writes nothing.
  • A far too long "ITS2" between distant anchors. ITSx takes an SSU-end anchor and an LSU-start anchor that lie far apart on the contig. Between them lies an anchor for the end of a 5.8S, but none for its start. ITSx then reports Start of 5.8S sequence not found; ITS region is suspiciously long (> 1500 bp) and writes no ITS1. Everything from that 5.8S end to the LSU start is written as ITS2, so SINTAX classifies a long stretch of genome as if it were an ITS2.

ITSx's --allow_reorder option changes the outcome in neither case.

docs.title: What the windows change
docs.text:
The turn of each window fixes the failed strand decision, and the window size, together with the length limits, keeps a false ITS2 out of the classification.

  • The turn. Each window is turned to read from SSU to LSU before ITSx sees it.
  • The window size. A window of 4,001 bp holds part of one rDNA unit only. The 2 kb on each side of the 5.8S gene hold the SSU end and the LSU start, around an ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 region of 0.4 to 1.5 kb.
  • The length limits. ITS1 or ITS2 outside 50 to 600 bp is listed in {sample}_ITS_copies.txt and not classified, and this is what keeps a false ITS2 out of SINTAX. A full ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 region longer than its.max_full_length (1,500 bp by default) is marked rejected_too_long in the same table. The full region itself is never classified. That default is the length above which ITSx itself calls an ITS region "suspiciously long".

Windows from the minus strand fail too unless they are turned

Without the turn, windows from the minus strand fail in the same way as whole minus-strand contigs. The cause of that failure is how ITSx handles the strand, not the tandem copies or the window size.

docs.title: The Medaka model
docs.text:
Medaka polishes an ONT assembly with the ONT reads, and its model must match the basecaller model that produced them. FunFlux checks a named model, or works the model out from the raw reads, before the assembler starts. A wrong model therefore stops the run within seconds instead of after the assembly.

Only ONT samples in longread and hybrid mode run Medaka, and PacBio HiFi samples never do. On Botrytis cinerea B05.10, Medaka removed 289 indels, 15 % of those in the assembly, and added 14 mismatches (Medaka on the 42x run).

---
config:
  themeVariables:
    fontSize: 14px
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 35
    rankSpacing: 35
---
flowchart TD
    R([raw ONT reads]) --> C[check or work out the model<br/>check_medaka_model<br/>auto: from the read headers]
    C --> F([sample_medaka_model.txt])
    F --> A[hifiasm or Flye<br/>starts only after the check]
    A --> M[Medaka polishing<br/>of the screened assembly<br/>with the model in that file]
    F --> M

Terms used on this page

Medaka model the trained model Medaka polishes an ONT assembly with; FunFlux checks it before the assembler starts basecaller model the model the ONT basecaller called the bases with; the Medaka model must match it basecaller tag the basecall_model_version_id= field in ONT read headers, which names the basecaller model; with medaka_model: auto, Medaka reads it from the first 100 reads consensus model a Medaka model for polishing an assembly, as opposed to Medaka's variant-calling models; with auto, FunFlux asks Medaka for its generic consensus model model weights the trained numbers that make up a model; Medaka downloads those of models it does not ship rule one step of the workflow as Snakemake defines it, such as check_medaka_model; the console and the log files in logs/ use its name guide assembly the SPAdes assembly of the Illumina reads; it is screened, and only the pairs that map to it go on Flye read mode the Flye option for the read type: --pacbio-hifi for every PacBio sample, --nano-hq or --nano-raw for ONT samples

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The Medaka keys go in the block named after the mode, parameters.longread or parameters.hybrid. medaka_model chooses the model, or switches Medaka off:

medaka_model Effect auto (the default; also empty or an unquoted null, true, yes, on, 1) the model is worked out from the read headers a Medaka model name, for example r1041_e82_400bps_sup_v4.3.0 that model, once the check has found it in the installed Medaka the path of a model file that file, as it is false (also 0, no, off, none, null in quotes) no Medaka for any sample. longread mode then delivers the screened assembly unpolished, while hybrid mode still polishes it with Polypolish

medaka_model_fallback_auto (default false) decides what happens when a named model is not available. With true, the check works the model out from the reads instead of stopping the run.

When the workflow starts, it prints one of these lines:

Line When Medaka model: <name>. a model is named and the batch has ONT samples Medaka model will be worked out from the FASTQ headers (checked before assembly). auto, and the batch has ONT samples Medaka disabled in the config. Skipping consensus polishing. false, and the batch has ONT samples No ONT samples in this batch: any medaka_model setting is ignored. only PacBio samples

docs.title: How the model is checked or worked out
docs.text:
The check is rule check_medaka_model, which runs once for every ONT sample that uses Medaka, in the Medaka 2.2.2 environment on one thread. It writes the model to 02.assembly/{sample}/{sample}_medaka_model.txt. The assembly of that sample waits for this file, while PacBio samples do not wait. A changed medaka_model therefore re-runs the check, the assembly of every ONT sample and everything after it.

After the assembly, the polishing rule long_read_consensus runs medaka_consensus -m with the model in that file, so the check and the polishing always use the same model. A named model and auto are checked in different ways:

A named model auto How it is checked or found compared with the list that medaka tools list_models prints medaka tools resolve_model --auto_model consensus <raw reads> What goes into the file the name, unchanged the path of the model file Network, for the check needed once, unless Medaka ships the model. Once the name has passed, the check downloads the model weights from GitHub (medaka tools download_models), and later runs reuse the stored copy needed once. The first time Medaka meets a model that is not installed, it downloads the model weights from GitHub, and later runs reuse the stored copy What the reads need no basecaller tag needed exactly one basecaller model among the first 100 reads

With auto, Medaka reads the basecaller model from the basecall_model_version_id= tag in the headers of the first 100 reads and returns the matching consensus model. FunFlux asks Medaka for its generic consensus model. Medaka reads .fastq.gz directly and stops after 100 records, so the call takes a few seconds whatever the size of the read file.

auto therefore needs one basecaller tag in the read headers. Reads from public archives, reads whose headers were rewritten, and reads pooled from several basecalling runs often lack the tag or mix two. Name the model for them.

The check reads the raw reads, not Filtlong's output, because the filtered reads can come late. In hybrid mode with short_read_guidance: true, they exist only after the Illumina guide assembly and its contamination and mitochondrion screen, hours into the run.

To see what the raw reads carry, print the header of the first read:

zcat /path/to/reads/SAMPLE_ont.fastq.gz | head -n 1

docs.title: What can fail
docs.text:
When the check fails, it writes its messages to its log, prints the log to the console and stops the run (exit status 1) before the assembly:

Situation Message What to do auto, and Medaka cannot work out a model ERROR: Medaka could not infer a model from the reads: their FASTQ headers carry no basecaller tag, or one this Medaka version does not recognise. Set parameters.<mode>.medaka_model to one of the consensus models below (pick by your flowcell / device / accuracy), or to FALSE to skip Medaka. name the model, or set false a named model that the installed Medaka does not have ERROR: Configured medaka_model '<name>' is not available in this Medaka version. correct the name from the table that follows the same, with medaka_model_fallback_auto: true, and auto also fails ERROR: Configured medaka_model '<name>' is not available, and fallback auto-inference could not infer a usable model from the reads. name an available model a named model that exists, whose weights are not stored and cannot be downloaded ERROR: Medaka model '<name>' exists, but its weights are not stored on this computer and could not be downloaded (Medaka downloads them from GitHub). ... start Snakemake on a computer with internet (on a cluster the check runs where Snakemake runs), or name a model whose weights come with Medaka 2.2.2 (r1041_e82_400bps_hac_v6.0.0 or r1041_e82_400bps_sup_v5.2.0), or set false medaka tools list_models gives no answer Could not read the Medaka model list ('medaka tools list_models' gave no 'Available:' line). rebuild the Medaka environment

Except for the download failure, each ERROR is followed by a table of consensus models with the columns model, flowcell, device, accuracy and version. For a mistyped name, the table is narrowed to the models that share the flowcell, device and accuracy written in that name. Otherwise it lists every model that medaka tools list_models reports except the variant-calling ones. The table can include special-purpose models, such as the bacterial methylation and plant models, which are not meant for fungi.

The auto message hides Medaka's own error

Any failure of medaka tools resolve_model gives the first message above, including two different basecaller tags in the first 100 reads and a download of the weights that failed. Check the read headers and the network before you name a model.

With medaka_model_fallback_auto: true and a named model that is not available, the run goes on with the inferred model, and the log says:

WARNING: configured medaka_model '<name>' is not available in this Medaka version; fell back to the auto-inferred model '<model>' (parameters.<mode>.medaka_model_fallback_auto is on). Set medaka_model to auto to silence this.

On success, the log shows Medaka model resolved to: <model>.

docs.title: Medaka model and Flye read mode
docs.text:
With assembler: flye, the Medaka model can choose the Flye read mode of the ONT samples. To choose the Flye mode independently of the Medaka model, set flye_input_mode to nano-hq or nano-raw.

flye_input_mode medaka_model Flye mode of the ONT samples auto a named model with fast in its name --nano-raw auto anything else, including auto, which never changes the Flye mode --nano-hq nano-hq or nano-raw any that mode

docs.title: Run-to-run differences
docs.text:
Two FunFlux runs on the same input, with the same settings, databases and conda environments, do not always write the same files. This page records which steps repeat exactly, which do not, why, and what FunFlux does about it. It is a running record, and the page says so wherever a step has not been checked yet.

The differences matter when you compare two runs, for example before and after changing a setting. A difference that also appears when the same setting is run twice is not caused by the setting. Compare genome files byte for byte, but compare gene models, and everything computed from them, with some tolerance. When the difference matters, run each setting at least twice.

A step was checked by running it twice on the same input and comparing its output files, byte for byte or, for gene models, model by model. A gene model counts as identical when all its coding intervals (exons, start and stop) agree.

Terms used on this page

identical gene model a gene model with the same coding intervals in two runs: every exon, the start and the stop random seed the number a program's random choices start from; fixing it makes a later run repeat the same choices BUSCO training genes the BUSCO genes funannotate looks for to train SNAP, GlimmerHMM and, without a stored AUGUSTUS model, AUGUSTUS Tiberius a deep-learning gene finder with a fungi model its authors trained on many fungal genomes; on by default, it adds its gene models to funannotate's evidence Perl hash order the order in which Perl lists the entries of a lookup table (a hash); it changes from run to run unless PERL_HASH_SEED=0 fixes it self-training gene finder a gene finder that learns its parameters from the genome it annotates, with no stored model; GeneMark-ES works this way EVidenceModeler the program inside funannotate predict that builds one consensus gene per locus from the gene finders and protein alignments, weighting each source's votes matching gene a FunFlux gene whose coding part has the same introns as a reference transcript, start and stop aside; an intronless gene matches on near-complete overlap

docs.title: Steps that repeat exactly
docs.text:
The steps below gave the same result in both runs. Where one of their files is not identical byte for byte, it differs only in a path, a start time or the order of its lines, as the remarks say.

Step Rule What was compared Remark Contig filtering filter_contigs the FASTA, byte for byte funannotate clean and sort funannotate_preprocess the FASTA files, byte for byte the result does not depend on the number of CPUs tantan masking repeat_masking with masking_method: tantan the masked genome, byte for byte QUAST genome_assembly_evaluation the report files, byte for byte BUSCO of the genome completeness the scores the summary files print the path of the input, which changes with the output folder ITS windows, ITSx and SINTAX its_windows, its_extraction, its_classification the sequences and the classification SINTAX runs with a fixed random seed (--randseed 1) on one thread; ITSx's summary file also prints its start time funannotate's BUSCO training genes and SNAP inside funannotate_prediction busco.final.gff3 and the SNAP predictions, byte for byte Protein alignments and AUGUSTUS inside funannotate_prediction the coordinates the files list the same lines in a different order Tiberius tiberius_prediction the GTF, byte for byte two runs on the same genome, with 25 and 32 threads; TensorFlow warns at start-up that its CPU maths may give slightly different numbers, but here they did not change the gene models Tiberius's GTF converted to GFF3 tiberius_gff3 the GFF3, byte for byte FunFlux fixes Perl's hash order (PERL_HASH_SEED=0, see EVidenceModeler below) MultiQC multiqc the numbers two of its data files hold absolute paths

docs.title: Steps that do not repeat exactly
docs.text:
In two FunFlux runs on the same input, the steps below do not give the same result. The table gives what differs, the cause where it was traced, and what FunFlux does about it.

Step What differs Why What FunFlux does RepeatModeler (masking_method: repeatmodeler_repeatmasker) the repeat library, and with it the masking and the genes predicted after it RepeatModeler takes a random sample of the genome and seeds it from the clock setting parameters.repeatmodeler_seed fixes the seed (-srand). Whether the whole annotation then repeats has not been checked. The default, tantan, repeats exactly. GeneMark-ES, inside funannotate_prediction its gene predictions its self-training on the genome does not repeat exactly; the cause inside GeneMark-ES was not traced nothing, because GeneMark-ES has no seed option GlimmerHMM, inside funannotate_prediction its gene predictions not traced nothing EVidenceModeler 1.1.1, inside funannotate_prediction the consensus gene at some loci, even when its inputs hold the same predictions where two gene structures score the same, EVidenceModeler takes the one that comes first in a Perl hash (a lookup table), and Perl lists a hash in an order that changes from run to run. funannotate also writes EVidenceModeler's input files in an order that changes from run to run. nothing yet. With Perl's hash order fixed (PERL_HASH_SEED=0 PERL_PERTURB_KEYS=0), EVidenceModeler gave the same result three times on one test region. Whether that makes the whole gene prediction repeat has not been checked. Everything computed from the predicted proteins: InterProScan, eggNOG-mapper, antiSMASH, SignalP 6, funannotate annotate the details they inherit the differences of the gene models nothing Flye (assembler: flye) the assembly Flye does not repeat its assembly byte for byte hifiasm is the default assembler

The final gene models of two runs on the same genome differ at a small share of the loci

Everything computed from the proteins inherits these differences. On the public genome Botrytis cinerea B05.10, two runs of the gene prediction on the same masked genome differed at 112 of 11,830 gene models, about 1 %. One run had 32 threads and the other 20. The number of genes that match the reference annotation went from 10,623 to 10,619. See Validation on public genomes.
